PROVA-MG: A Probabilistic Routing Framework for Low-Resource Malagasy Speech Recognition

DOCTORAL METHODOLOGY NOTE / ENGINEERING AND TECHNOLOGY SCIENCES

A unified methodology for Automatic Speech Recognition that aggregates heterogeneous foundation models, typological priors, and a large licensed unlabeled corpus under explicit calibration and explicit constraints, together with the validation procedure that supports its claims.

CandidateRANDRIAMANASINA Mianala Loharano
DirectorPr RAVONINJATOVO Achille Olivier
Co-directorDr Haingonirina Ignace RAJAOSOLOMANANTENA
SchoolDoctoral School 3D, University of Toamasina
Host teamEngineering and Technology Sciences
DisciplineComputer Engineering and Artificial Intelligence
StatusWorking draft, methodology proposal

Abstract

Malagasy is nominally covered by every modern multilingual ASR release, yet zero-shot quality is poor and no single foundation model, supervision regime, or adaptation technique improves it on its own.

PROVA-MG — Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy — treats low-resource ASR as a probabilistic system that aggregates heterogeneous evidence. Three foundation models (Whisper-large-v3, MMS, Wav2Vec2-BERT) are retained as distinct posteriors and their disagreement is used as a routing signal; an Austronesian typological prior constrains decoding where a Malagasy-only language model cannot; iterative pseudo-labeling is formalized as a constrained variational EM procedure with explicit non-collapse conditions; dialect, register, and code-switching are unified as latent variables; and a calibration head, trained on the small supervised set, ensures that every confidence feeding into the system is trustworthy.

The four chapters below carry the argument: the foundational state of the art, the multilingual and low-resource state of the art together with the open methodological gaps, the PROVA-MG methodology and its integration with the existing data pipeline, and the validation procedure, expected applications, and limitations.

BODY

General Introduction and Position of the Problem

PROVA-MG / General Introduction

The present introduction situates the work, defines its terms, surveys the state of knowledge in compact form, articulates the research problem and its underlying questions, states the hypotheses and the central objective, describes the methodology in outline, anticipates the expected results, and ends with the plan of the four chapters that follow.

OPENING

Hook: speech as the missing modality

For the more than twenty-five million speakers of Malagasy, the spoken language remains the medium of nearly every consequential daily exchange — in the household, in the marketplace, in the place of worship, in the courthouse, in the hospital, in the field. And yet, when those same speakers approach the digital tools that now mediate education, public administration, journalism, and commerce, they are systematically asked to type, in a register that may not be their own, in an orthography that may not match their dialect, on devices whose interfaces almost always presuppose a high-resource language. Speech, the natural modality, is the missing modality.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), the engineering discipline whose object is the transcription of an acoustic signal into text, has known three successive technical revolutions since the late 1980s. None of them has delivered, for Malagasy, an instrument whose Word Error Rate would make it usable in any of the practical settings just enumerated. The present thesis takes that gap as its starting point and asks under what conditions the gap may be closed without requiring resources that a low-resource setting, by definition, cannot mobilize.

STAKE — The stake of the present work is not merely the production of a transcription system but the demonstration that a probabilistically principled framework can extract, from heterogeneous evidence, the quality that no single model, dataset, or technique provides on its own.

SECTION 0.1

Definition of key terms

In order to delimit precisely the object of the present study, several terms used recurrently in what follows are defined here. The definitions are operational rather than theoretical; the corresponding theoretical content is developed in Chapter I.

0.1.1 Automatic Speech Recognition

By Automatic Speech Recognition is meant the family of computational procedures that take as input an acoustic signal — typically a digitized waveform sampled at sixteen kilohertz — and return as output a sequence of orthographic tokens (characters, sub-words, or words) intended to correspond to what a competent human listener would transcribe. The quality of an ASR system is measured, throughout the present work, by the Word Error Rate and the Character Error Rate, complemented for diagnostic purposes by paired bootstrap and Wilcoxon significance tests, by the Expected Calibration Error, and by per-dialect equity measures.

0.1.2 Low-resource language

A low-resource language is here understood to mean any language for which the available transcribed audio is at least one order of magnitude below the volume on which high-resource ASR systems are routinely trained, and for which the available unlabeled audio is heterogeneous, dialectally fragmented, and partially licensed. Malagasy, with fewer than five hundred publicly released hours of supervised audio at the moment of writing, falls unambiguously within this category.

0.1.3 Foundation model

A foundation model denotes, in the present text, a pre-trained neural network of substantial size (typically several hundred million parameters or more), released with weights, trained on a corpus that spans dozens to hundreds of languages, and intended to be adapted by fine-tuning or by inference-time conditioning. Three such models are central to the present methodology: Whisper-large-v3, MMS, and Wav2Vec2-BERT.

0.1.4 Probabilistic routing

By probabilistic routing is meant the operation that takes as input several approximate posterior distributions over transcripts — one per foundation model — together with their disagreement structure, and returns a categorical decision regarding the use of the segment: train-time inclusion, deferral to human review, reservation, or rejection. Routing is distinguished from averaging: averaging is appropriate when posteriors are mutually calibrated, which empirically is not the case for heterogeneous foundation models on a low-resource language.

SECTION 0.2

Context and state of knowledge

Two intersecting threads of context bear on the present work. The first is the linguistic and sociolinguistic situation of Malagasy. The second is the recent history of ASR for low-resource languages.

0.2.1 The linguistic situation of Malagasy

Malagasy is the easternmost member of the Austronesian family, sharing typological structure — agglutinative morphology, verb-initial word order, predicate-focused syntax — with Indonesian, Malay, Cebuano, and Tagalog. The standard orthography, codified in the nineteenth century, is based on the Merina dialect. The country, however, hosts at least eighteen recognized dialect groups, several of which (Betsimisaraka, Sakalava, Antandroy, Antaisaka) diverge substantially from the standard at the phonological, morphological, and lexical levels. The diglossia between standard Merina and French, the latter retained as a co-official language of administration and higher education, produces a pervasive code-switching that any realistic ASR system must accommodate.

0.2.2 The recent state of ASR for low-resource languages

Three lines of work have transformed the prospects of low-resource ASR over the past decade. First, large-scale self-supervised pre-training (Wav2Vec 2.0, HuBERT, WavLM) demonstrated that universal acoustic representations could be learned from unlabeled audio. Second, cross-lingual self-supervision (XLS-R, MMS, Wav2Vec2-BERT) extended that property to hundreds of languages simultaneously, with explicit coverage of low-resource members. Third, weak supervision at web scale (Whisper) demonstrated that imperfectly paired audio-text data could substitute for clean transcripts at the cost of additional volume. Each of these lines nominally covers Malagasy. None of them, taken alone, delivers a deployable system.

0.2.3 The unresolved core

Beyond these three lines, four methodological questions remain open at the moment of writing. They are: (i) the principled probabilistic integration of multiple heterogeneous foundation models; (ii) the injection of typological priors drawn from a known language family; (iii) the formal treatment of iterative pseudo-labeling under non-collapse conditions; (iv) the unification of dialect, register, and code-switching as latent variables. The present thesis takes those four questions as the scaffolding of its methodological contribution.

SECTION 0.3

Interest of the topic

The interest of the topic operates on three planes that the present introduction takes care to distinguish.

0.3.1 Scientific interest

The scientific interest of the topic is that it forces a confrontation between the empiricism of contemporary deep learning and the inferential rigour of classical probabilistic modeling. The proposed framework re-reads pseudo-labeling, ensemble methods, and confidence calibration in a variational-Bayesian idiom that yields explicit convergence and non-collapse conditions; that re-reading, if it succeeds, contributes to the methodology of low-resource ASR irrespective of the specific language on which it is instantiated.

0.3.2 Technological interest

The technological interest is the production of a working transcription pipeline whose components are released under open licenses, accompanied by datasheets and model cards, and validated against frozen, dialect-stratified test sets. Such a release lowers the entry cost for further research and applied work in the same setting.

0.3.3 Societal interest

The societal interest is that a robust ASR system for Malagasy — understood as one that maintains usable performance across the principal dialects rather than only on the standard variety — enables a range of public-interest applications: educational support, accessibility services for visually impaired or low-literacy users, administrative transcription, journalistic indexing, and preservation of intangible oral heritage. The present work treats dialect equity as an explicit evaluation dimension precisely so that the societal claim can be tested rather than merely asserted.

SECTION 0.4

Research problem and research questions

The general research problem of the present thesis may be stated as follows. Under what conditions, and with what methodological apparatus, can the existing foundation models for multilingual speech recognition be combined with the available licensed Malagasy audio so as to yield a deployable ASR system whose performance is competitive on the standard variety, equitable across dialects, calibrated in its confidences, and reproducible from public artifacts?

That general problem decomposes into four ordered research questions, which structure the four chapters of the manuscript.

  • Q1. What probabilistic and neural foundations are available, and what is the structure of their formal relations? (Chapter I.)
  • Q2. How have those foundations been extended to multilingual and low-resource settings, and what methodological problems remain open? (Chapter II.)
  • Q3. How may those open problems be addressed in a unified framework that admits formal analysis and integrates with a license-first data substrate? (Chapter III.)
  • Q4. How is the resulting framework validated, what does the available evidence allow one to claim, and what limitations condition the interpretation of the expected results? (Chapter IV.)

SECTION 0.5

Hypotheses

Five working hypotheses are stated at the outset and tested by the validation procedure of Chapter IV.

  • H1 (heterogeneity). The disagreement structure of three heterogeneous foundation models on Malagasy carries information that is not recoverable from any single posterior.
  • H2 (typology). A phonotactic and morphotactic prior trained on the Austronesian family constrains decoding hypotheses in regions of the space that a Malagasy-only language model cannot constrain.
  • H3 (constrained EM). Iterative pseudo-labeling subject to a confidence floor, a KL drift bound, an agreement constraint, and a typological consistency constraint converges to a stationary point without the collapse observed in the unconstrained version.
  • H4 (latent variables). Treating dialect, register, and code-switching as latent variables in a single graphical model improves performance on under-represented dialects and on code-switched speech without degrading the majority dialect.
  • H5 (calibration). A post-hoc calibration head trained on a small supervised set generalizes to the larger, distributionally shifted unlabeled pool with substantially lower Expected Calibration Error than uncalibrated confidences.

SECTION 0.6

Objective

The general objective of the present thesis is to formulate, instantiate, and validate PROVA-MG — Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy — a unified probabilistic framework for low-resource ASR comprising five interlocking components, and to demonstrate, on three independent, frozen, dialect-stratified test sets, that the framework outperforms every subset of its components and every published baseline.

That general objective decomposes into the following specific objectives:

  • Construct a license-first, dialect-balanced Malagasy speech corpus, with provenance metadata, datasheets, and a persistent DOI.
  • Implement the routing function of Component 3.1 and demonstrate, by ablation, that routing outperforms averaging and voting.
  • Implement and evaluate the typological prior of Component 3.2, reporting the result whether positive or negative.
  • Implement the constrained variational EM of Component 3.3, derive its convergence and non-collapse conditions, and verify them empirically.
  • Implement the latent-variable decomposition of Component 3.4 and verify, by stratified evaluation, that it improves dialect equity.
  • Implement the calibration head of Component 3.5 and verify its generalization across the distribution shift between the supervised and the unlabeled set.
  • Release the corpus, the models, the code, and the reproducibility bundles under open licenses.

SECTION 0.7

Methodology in outline

The methodology of the present thesis is empirically oriented but formally constrained. Its outline is as follows.

The data substrate is constructed through a nine-stage license-first pipeline that produces a Tier-A gold supervised set, a Tier-B silver set, a Tier-C licensed unlabeled set, and a Tier-D restricted set, each accompanied by provenance and licensing metadata. Three foundation models — Whisper-large-v3, MMS, and Wav2Vec2-BERT — are retained as distinct posteriors over the transcript; their disagreement structure is used as the input to a learned routing function trained on the supervised set. An Austronesian typological prior is trained on Indonesian, Malay, Cebuano, and Tagalog text and integrated into decoding through a calibrated mixture. Iterative pseudo-labeling is formalized as a constrained variational EM procedure whose E-step minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the variational posterior and the model posterior subject to four explicit constraints, and whose M-step maximizes the expected complete-data log-likelihood. Dialect, register, and code-switching are treated as latent variables in a single graphical model that admits joint approximate inference. A post-hoc calibration head, trained on the supervised set with features drawn from model entropy, three-way agreement, typological likelihood, segment duration, voice-activity confidence, and dialect-posterior entropy, produces the confidences consumed by every downstream constraint.

The validation procedure is structured as eight phases, each terminated by a measurable gate, as detailed in Chapter IV.

SECTION 0.8

Expected results

The expected results are organized along four axes. On the axis of headline performance, the integrated PROVA-MG system is expected to reduce WER on FLEURS-MG, CV-MG, and the in-domain test set by a margin that paired bootstrap and Wilcoxon tests confirm to be statistically significant relative to every baseline. On the axis of dialect equity, performance on Betsimisaraka, Sakalava, and Antandroy is expected to improve without degradation of Merina. On the axis of calibration, the Expected Calibration Error of the calibrated confidence is expected to be substantially lower than that of the raw confidence, with the calibrator trained on the supervised set generalizing to the unlabeled distribution. On the axis of methodological robustness, each constraint of the variational EM is expected to contribute a measurable share of the total gain, and the unconstrained loop is expected to demonstrably collapse where the constrained loop does not.

CAVEAT — The above expectations are working hypotheses to be confirmed or refuted by the validation procedure of Chapter IV. A negative result on any single component is recorded as such and reported in the manuscript and in the corresponding paper.

SECTION 0.9

Plan of the thesis

The remainder of the thesis is organized in four chapters, each opened by a brief introduction, structured around two main parts (themselves divided into three subsections), and closed by a chapter conclusion. A general conclusion, a bibliography, eight appendices, the candidate information sheet, and the French and English abstracts complete the manuscript.

  • Chapter I — Foundations of speech recognition. The four paradigms (classical HMM-GMM, hybrid DNN-HMM, end-to-end neural, self-supervised representation) are reviewed in compact form together with the mathematics that connects them.
  • Chapter II — Low-resource and multilingual ASR. The methods that extend the four paradigms to multilingual and low-resource settings are surveyed, the data substrate of the present work is described, and the open methodological problems are identified.
  • Chapter III — The PROVA-MG methodology. The five components of the framework are derived, their algorithmic implementation is specified, their complexity is analysed, and their integration with the data substrate is described.
  • Chapter IV — Application, results and discussion. The prototype implementation, the planned experimental matrix, the expected results in placeholder form, the discussion of limitations and threats to validity, and the perspectives of further work are presented.

Chapter I — Foundations of Speech Recognition

PROVA-MG / Chapter I of IV

Chapter I: Foundations of Speech Recognition

This first chapter reviews the classical and neural foundations on which contemporary speech recognition is built. It is organized in two main parts: the classical and hybrid paradigms, then the neural and self-supervised paradigms. Each part develops three subsections in mathematical detail.

CHAPTER INTRODUCTION

From acoustics to text: the probabilistic substrate

Automatic Speech Recognition is, in its modern formulation, the inversion of a noisy generative channel. Let X denote the observed acoustic feature sequence and W the underlying word sequence. The Bayesian decomposition

P(W | X) = (P(X | W) P(W))/(P(X))

has organized the discipline since Jelinek and Bahl (1976) and remains, in spirit if not always in letter, the structuring principle of every paradigm reviewed below. The acoustic term P(X | W) describes how a word sequence generates a feature stream; the language-model term P(W) describes the prior plausibility of a sequence; the marginal P(X) serves only as a normalizing constant in the argmax. ASR has evolved by progressively replacing each of the three terms by learned components while retaining the formal architecture of the decomposition.

Four broadly successive paradigms structure the field. The classical HMM-GMM paradigm modelled both the acoustic emission and the temporal dynamics by hand-crafted, generatively trained probabilistic components. The hybrid DNN-HMM paradigm retained the temporal HMM scaffolding and replaced the Gaussian emission by a discriminatively trained neural network. The end-to-end neural paradigm collapsed the modular pipeline into a single network mapping acoustics to text. The self-supervised representation paradigm shifted the bottleneck from supervision to representation by pre-training large encoders on unlabeled audio. Each paradigm absorbed rather than discarded its predecessor: a contemporary system, in particular the systems on which the present thesis is built, exhibits traces of all four. The chapter that follows develops each paradigm in turn, with attention to the mathematics that bears on the methodology of Chapter III.

PART ONE — A

I.1 Classical and hybrid paradigms

The classical and hybrid paradigms share the modular architecture inherited from Bahl, Jelinek, and Mercer: an acoustic model, a pronunciation lexicon, a language model, and a decoder. Their successive variants differ in how the acoustic model is parameterized and trained.

I.1.1 The classical paradigm: HMM-GMM

The hidden Markov model with Gaussian-mixture emissions (HMM-GMM) modelled speech as a hidden discrete Markov chain whose states emit, at each time step, observations drawn from a Gaussian mixture density over short-frame features (MFCC, PLP). For a state sequence s = (s₁, …, s_T) and a feature sequence X = (x₁, …, x_T), the joint likelihood factorizes as

P(X, s | W) = ∏ₜ a(sₜ₋₁, sₜ) b_(sₜ)(xₜ)

where a(·,·) are transition probabilities and bₛ(·) are state-dependent emission densities, each itself a Gaussian mixture. Parameters were estimated by the Baum-Welch algorithm, an instance of Expectation-Maximization (EM) whose E-step computes occupation probabilities via the forward-backward recursion and whose M-step re-estimates means, covariances, and mixture weights in closed form.

Three features of HMM-GMM deserve mention because they recur in subsequent paradigms. First, the noisy-channel decomposition was operationalized through the explicit composition of acoustic, lexical, and language-model components. Second, decoding was formalized as a shortest-path search over a Weighted Finite-State Transducer (WFST) obtained by composing the HMM transducer H, the context-dependency transducer C, the lexicon transducer L, and the language-model transducer G:

Decoding graph: D = H ∘ C ∘ L ∘ G

That composition remains, in form, the formal substrate of contemporary beam search. Third, EM as the parameter estimation procedure introduced a vocabulary — latent variables, posterior responsibilities, the contrast between observed and complete-data likelihood — which the methodology of Chapter III inherits in its variational form.

I.1.2 The hybrid paradigm: DNN-HMM, TDNN-F, LF-MMI

Beginning with the work of Hinton, Deng, and Yu around 2009 and continuing through Kaldi-era systems, deep neural networks replaced the Gaussian mixture as the emission model while the decoder, the lexicon, and the language model remained external. Architecturally, this consisted in training a neural network to predict the posterior P(s | xₜ) of an HMM state given the acoustic frame, then converting the posterior to a scaled likelihood through Bayes' rule:

b_(sₜ)(xₜ) ∝ (P(s | xₜ))/(P(s))

where P(s) is the state prior estimated from the training alignments. The training of the network required an initial alignment, typically produced by an HMM-GMM system, and proceeded by minimization of the frame-level cross-entropy.

Three refinements have proven enduring. The time-delay neural network (TDNN) introduced by Peddinti, Povey, and Khudanpur (2015) replaced the dense feed-forward layers by sub-sampled, dilated convolutions over time, giving access to long contextual windows at moderate cost. The factorized variant TDNN-F, by inserting a low-rank linear bottleneck between successive TDNN layers, controlled over-fitting in low-data regimes. Lattice-free Maximum Mutual Information (LF-MMI), introduced by Povey and colleagues (2016), replaced the frame cross-entropy by a sequence-discriminative criterion computed without lattices, on a denominator graph that approximates the language-model marginal:

F_(MMI)(θ) = ∑ᵤ log (P_θ(Xᵤ | Wᵤ) P(Wᵤ))/(Z_θ(Xᵤ))

Hybrid systems remain competitive on small supervised sets, particularly when phonetic resources (pronunciation dictionaries, decision trees) are already available. They are engineering-intensive: each stage of the pipeline must be tuned and the dependency chain is long. They do not, on their own, address the multilingual or low-resource extension.

I.1.3 Decoding: WFST search and the lexicon

Both HMM-GMM and DNN-HMM rely on a single decoding apparatus: weighted finite-state transducer search. The decoding graph D = H ° C ° L ° G is determinized and minimized offline; at run time, a beam-pruned Viterbi search produces a lattice from which n-best lists, confusion networks, and posterior word probabilities can be extracted. The pronunciation lexicon L is the only component of the chain that requires explicit linguistic knowledge; for low-resource languages it is also typically the bottleneck. The methodology of Chapter III does not rely on a pronunciation lexicon, but inherits from the WFST tradition the habit of expressing language priors as composable weighted transducers.

PART ONE — B

I.2 Neural and self-supervised paradigms

The second part of the chapter addresses the two paradigms in which the modular pipeline of the classical and hybrid systems is replaced or relegated to a pre-training stage. End-to-end models collapse the pipeline into a single trainable network; self-supervised models shift the bottleneck from supervision to representation.

I.2.1 End-to-end objectives: CTC, attention, RNN-T

Three training objectives still structure the end-to-end family. They differ in how they relate the unaligned target sequence y = (y₁, …, y_U) to the frame sequence X = (x₁, …, x_T), with T ≫ U.

Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC, Graves et al. 2006) introduces an additional blank symbol and marginalizes over all monotonic, many-to-one alignments π : {1,…,T} → Y ∪ {blank} that collapse to y:

L_(CTC)(θ) = -log ∑_(π : B(π)=y) ∏ₜ P_θ(πₜ | xₜ)

The forward-backward recursion over the alignment lattice makes the gradient tractable. CTC converges rapidly, has few hyperparameters, and tolerates small supervised sets — properties that make it the dominant choice in low-resource ASR pipelines.

Attention-based encoder-decoder models (Listen, Attend and Spell; Chan et al. 2016) drop the monotonic assumption. An encoder produces a hidden sequence h = (h₁, …, h_T); an autoregressive decoder generates y token by token, attending at each step to a context cᵤ:

cᵤ = ∑ₜ α_(u,t) hₜ, α_(u,t) = softmaxₜ( e(sᵤ, hₜ) ) P(yᵤ | y_(<u), X) = decoder(sᵤ, cᵤ, yᵤ₋₁)

The loss is the cross-entropy of the target tokens. Attention models are more expressive than CTC but more data-hungry; they require regularization mechanisms (label smoothing, scheduled sampling, joint CTC-attention training) to remain stable on small supervised sets.

RNN Transducer (Graves 2012, Battenberg et al. 2017) re-introduces a monotonic alignment through an internal predictor network. A joint network combines the encoder state and the predictor state to produce

P(yᵤ | y_(<u), x_(1:t)) = softmax( W_z φ( hₜ , pᵤ ) )

The lattice over (t, u) admits an efficient forward-backward recursion and a streaming-compatible decoder. RNN-T is the production choice for low-latency recognition.

I.2.2 The Conformer encoder

The encoder of choice in contemporary end-to-end systems is the Conformer (Gulati et al. 2020), which combines convolution and self-attention in a single block. Each Conformer block applies, in order: a macaron feed-forward sub-layer; multi-head self-attention with relative positional encoding; a depthwise-separable convolution module; a second macaron feed-forward sub-layer; layer normalization. The block-level update may be written as

x ← x + 1/2 FFN(x) x ← x + MHSA(x) x ← x + Conv(x) x ← x + 1/2 FFN(x) x ← LayerNorm(x)

Self-attention captures long-range dependencies while the convolution module captures local patterns over a few tens of frames. The Conformer encoder underlies most of the foundation models reviewed in Chapter II and, in particular, the Wav2Vec2-BERT model that serves as one of the three teachers in the methodology of Chapter III.

I.2.3 Self-supervised representations: Wav2Vec 2.0, HuBERT, WavLM, data2vec

Self-supervised pre-training on unlabeled audio shifted the bottleneck from supervision to representation. The contrastive objective of Wav2Vec 2.0 (Baevski et al. 2020) masks a fraction of the convolutional features and asks the Transformer to identify, among a set of distractors qₖ, the quantized target qₜ aligned with the masked position:

L_(W2V2) = -log (exp (sim(cₜ, qₜ)/τ))/(∑ₖ exp (sim(cₜ, qₖ)/τ))

where cₜ is the contextual representation at the masked position, sim is cosine similarity, and τ is a temperature.

HuBERT (Hsu et al. 2021) replaced the contrastive term by masked prediction over discretized targets obtained by iterative k-means clustering of MFCCs (first iteration) or of the model's own intermediate representations (subsequent iterations). The objective becomes a standard cross-entropy over a finite codebook:

L_(HuBERT) = -∑_(t ∈ M) log P_θ( zₜ | cₜ )

WavLM (Chen et al. 2022) added a denoising pre-training signal by overlapping the input with noise and asking the model to predict the targets of the clean stream. data2vec (Baevski et al. 2022) replaced both discrete and contrastive targets by self-distilled latent representations of the unmasked input, computed by an exponential moving average of the student.

The practical value of these models for low-resource ASR is that fine-tuning a small CTC head on a few hours of supervised audio often matches the performance of a system trained from scratch on substantially larger supervised corpora. The four models listed above are nominally usable for Malagasy; Wav2Vec2-BERT, the cross-lingual variant pre-trained on Wav2Vec 2.0 plus BERT-style masked language modelling, serves as one of the three teachers retained in Chapter III.

CHAPTER CONCLUSION

Conclusion of Chapter I

The four paradigms reviewed in the present chapter share, in spite of their architectural differences, a single inferential skeleton: the inversion of a noisy generative channel under a learned acoustic likelihood and a learned language-model prior. Each paradigm refined that skeleton on one of its sides — the acoustic model first, the language-model integration next, the representation last. Each paradigm, however, is predominantly designed and evaluated on high-resource languages. Chapter II examines how the four paradigms extend to multilingual and low-resource settings, identifies the four open methodological problems on which the present thesis is centred, and describes the data substrate constructed for the empirical instantiation on Malagasy.

TRANSITION — Chapter I has supplied the formal vocabulary in which the methodology of Chapter III will be expressed. Chapter II supplies the empirical and methodological context in which that methodology becomes necessary.

Chapter II — Low-Resource and Multilingual ASR

PROVA-MG / Chapter II of IV

Chapter II: Low-Resource and Multilingual ASR

The present chapter surveys the methods that extend the four paradigms of Chapter I to multilingual and low-resource settings, describes the data substrate of the present work, identifies the open methodological problems, and prepares the methodological contribution of Chapter III.

CHAPTER INTRODUCTION

Why the four paradigms do not close the gap

The four paradigms reviewed in Chapter I are, in spite of their successive refinements, predominantly designed for and evaluated on high-resource languages. When transferred to a low-resource language such as Malagasy, each of them exhibits a characteristic failure mode. Classical and hybrid systems require pronunciation dictionaries and decision trees whose construction is costly. Attention-based end-to-end systems are too data-hungry to converge on the few hundred hours of supervised Malagasy currently available. Self-supervised representations close part of the gap by reducing the supervision requirement at fine-tuning time, but no single self-supervised model, fine-tuned on Malagasy alone, has been reported to attain the WER thresholds required by deployment.

The methods reviewed in the present chapter address that gap from three angles: by sharing representation across languages (cross-lingual self-supervision and weak supervision), by adapting large models efficiently (LoRA, adapters, prompts), and by exploiting unlabeled data through pseudo-labeling. The chapter then describes the data substrate of the present thesis, lists the foundation models retained, and concludes by enumerating the open methodological problems that motivate the framework of Chapter III.

PART TWO — A

II.1 Cross-lingual and multilingual methods

The first part of the chapter addresses the three families of methods that produce a single model usable across many languages.

II.1.1 Cross-lingual self-supervised representations

The earliest cross-lingual self-supervised model, XLSR-53 (Conneau et al. 2020), extended Wav2Vec 2.0 to a multilingual setting by joint pre-training on 53 languages drawn from CommonVoice, BABEL, and MLS. XLS-R (Babu et al. 2022) scaled the same recipe to 128 languages and 436 000 hours of unlabeled audio, and is the standard reference for cross-lingual self-supervised speech models at the time of writing. MMS (Pratap et al. 2023, Meta AI) further scaled to more than 1 100 languages, primarily through the alignment of religious text recordings (the New Testament corpus) supplemented by other licensed sources. Wav2Vec2-BERT (Seamless Communication 2024) combines a Wav2Vec 2.0 encoder pre-trained on roughly 4.5 million hours with a BERT-style masked language modelling head trained jointly on text, producing a model that doubles as a speech encoder and as a phonetic representation extractor.

All four of these models nominally cover Malagasy. Their zero-shot WER on FLEURS-MG is, however, high — typically far above the threshold of usability — and varies substantially across the dialects represented in the test set.

II.1.2 Large-scale weak supervision: Whisper and its variants

Whisper (Radford et al. 2023) takes a different approach. Instead of self-supervised pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning, it trains a single encoder-decoder on 680 000 hours of audio paired with weakly supervised transcripts collected from the open web. The training objective is straightforward cross-entropy on the paired data, with special tokens that distinguish languages, tasks (transcription, translation), and conditions (no-speech, timestamp).

USM (Universal Speech Model, Zhang et al. 2023, Google), Canary (NVIDIA), OWSM (Open Whisper-style Speech Model, ESPnet community), and OLMoASR are subsequent variants or open reimplementations. Whisper-large-v3 currently produces the strongest open zero-shot transcripts for Malagasy and is therefore used as the first-pass teacher in the pipeline of the present work.

II.1.3 Speech-LLMs and unified models

Recent systems feed speech to a large language model either as discrete tokens or through a learned projection (SALMONN, Qwen-Audio, Phi-4-Multimodal). For high-resource languages, quality rivals that of dedicated ASR. For low-resource languages, performance is bounded above by the text-side coverage of the underlying LLM; for Malagasy in particular, the text coverage of contemporary LLMs is uneven and the resulting transcripts exhibit characteristic hallucinations on low-frequency lexical items. The present work does not place speech-LLMs on the load-bearing path of the methodology, but considers them as candidates for a future comparison.

PART TWO — B

II.2 Adaptation, pseudo-labeling, and license-first data

The second part of the chapter addresses the three families of methods that adapt or supplement a pre-trained model with target-language resources, and presents the data substrate constructed for the present thesis.

II.2.1 Parameter-efficient adaptation: LoRA, adapters, prompts

Full fine-tuning of a foundation model with several hundred million parameters on a few hundred hours of Malagasy audio is computationally expensive and risks over-fitting. Parameter-efficient adaptation methods address both concerns. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022) inserts a trainable low-rank update Δ W = B A alongside the frozen weight matrix W:

y = W x + B A x

where A and B have rank r much smaller than the model dimension. Adapter layers (Houlsby et al. 2019) insert small bottleneck residual modules after each Transformer sub-layer. BitFit trains only the biases. Prompt tuning learns soft prefixes prepended to the input. For low-resource ASR these methods reduce both GPU cost and over-fitting risk, and they admit composition: language-specific LoRA adapters can be combined with dialect-specific adapters, which is the route taken in Component 3.4 of Chapter III.

II.2.2 Semi-supervised learning, pseudo-labeling, and self-training

Iterative pseudo-labeling (ITP) and its variants — slimIPL (Likhomanenko et al. 2021), Kaizen (Manohar et al. 2021), Noisy Student (Park et al. 2020), momentum pseudo-labeling (Khurana et al. 2022), the massively multilingual pseudo-labeling regime of Hsu et al. (2022) — share a common procedure. A seed model is trained on the supervised set, transcribes the unlabeled pool, filters the resulting pseudo-labels by confidence, and is retrained on the union of supervised and filtered pseudo-labeled data. Variations concern the filtering criterion (raw confidence, posterior entropy, agreement between augmented versions), the teacher-update rule (replacement at each iteration, exponential moving average, fixed teacher), and the prevention of collapse (confidence thresholds, KL drift bounds, noise injection on the student). Recent extensions to foundation models include uDistil-Whisper (Park, Berrebbi et al. 2024), STAR for unsupervised adaptation of speech foundation models (Hu et al. 2024), and large-scale pseudo-labeling for low-resource Indic ASR (Bhogale et al. 2024). The empirical collapse phenomenon — rising confidence accompanied by accuracy degradation — is documented systematically by Likhomanenko, Lugosch & Collobert (2023) for continuous soft pseudo-labels, and is the empirical motivation for the constraints introduced in Chapter III.

Beyond ASR, the theoretical reading of pseudo-labeling as constrained posterior inference has been established for two decades. Posterior Regularization (Ganchev, Graça, Gillenwater & Taskar 2010) formalizes the E-step as q* = argmin KL(q || p_theta(. | x)) subject to expectation constraints, and Generalized Expectation Criteria (Mann & McCallum 2008, 2010) cast weakly supervised learning as imposing expectation constraints on the model posterior. Alternating projections (Bellare, Druck & McCallum 2009) and Unified EM (Samdani, Chang & Roth 2012) unify the parametric family of constrained-EM variants. Cross-lingual transfer with posterior regularization was demonstrated by Das & Petrov (2013). On the theoretical side, KL-constrained updates between iterates are a standard trust-region device (Schulman et al. 2015), and recent work has begun to characterize the non-collapse of iterative retraining of generative and discriminative models (Bertrand et al. 2024; Aubin et al. 2025; Wei, Shen, Chen & Ma 2021). Bayesian and uncertainty-aware self-training (Mukherjee & Awadallah 2020; Rizve et al. 2021; Lienen & Hüllermeier 2021; Rodemann et al. 2023) and the FixMatch / FlexMatch / FreeMatch confidence-threshold family (Sohn et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2023) constitute the immediate methodological neighbourhood. The present thesis re-formalizes iterative pseudo-labeling as a constrained variational EM procedure in Chapter III (Component 3.3); its constraint set instantiates posterior regularization for the ASR setting and adds a between-iteration KL drift bound together with an explicit non-collapse argument that, to our knowledge, are not stated in this combined form in the prior literature.

II.2.4 Multi-teacher and heterogeneous-teacher pseudo-labeling

System combination has a long history in ASR. ROVER (Fiscus 1997) combines the hypotheses of several recognizers by voting at the level of a confusion network. Confidence-based ensembles of end-to-end ASR models, in which the most-confident model's output is selected per utterance, were revisited by Gitman et al. (2023) and shown to beat dedicated language-identification routing. Knowledge distillation from multiple foundation models was explored by Yang et al. (2023) and, in the multilingual setting, by Yan et al. (2024) through simple N-best re-ranking. The recent literature on multi-ASR pseudo-labeling is the closest immediate antecedent of the heterogeneous co-inference of Chapter III. The Pratinidhi framework (Kulkarni et al. 2024) combines multiple ASR transcribers with agreement-based filtering, Rényi entropy, and a SONAR similarity evaluator; Carofilis et al. (2025) implement multi-domain consensus filtering across Whisper, Zipformer, and Parakeet by CER majority vote; Rangappa et al. (2025) propose multi-stage filtering of pseudo-labels generated by two teachers; Prakash et al. (2025) arbitrate three-way ASR disagreement with a speech-conditioned large language model. Together these works establish that aggregating several foundation-style teachers improves pseudo-label quality on low-resource and multi-domain ASR. None of them, however, treats the teachers as distinct posteriors within a probabilistic framework, none uses a learned router over their disagreement signal, and none combines Whisper-large-v3, MMS, and Wav2Vec2-BERT specifically; these gaps motivate Component 3.1.

II.2.5 Cross-family transfer and typological priors

External language models are conventionally integrated into ASR decoding through log-linear shallow fusion (Klakow 1998), revisited in the end-to-end era by Kannan et al. (2018) as the canonical analysis of external-LM fusion in sequence-to-sequence ASR. Cross-lingual and related-language LM rescoring for low-resource ASR has been demonstrated by Khare et al. (2024) for Indic languages and by Currey et al. (2024) for African code-switching. Massively multilingual adversarial ASR (Adams et al. 2019) and typologically aware rescoring (Chan et al. 2025) explicitly use typological features as a design principle, and Adilazuarda et al. (2024, LinguAlchemy) fuse typological and geographical features for unseen-language generalization. The URIEL/lang2vec typological knowledge base (Littell et al. 2017) and its extension URIEL+ (Khan et al. 2024) provide the standard machine-readable representation of language typology used in this line of work; Ponti et al. (2019) survey the broader use of typology in NLP. For the specifically Austronesian context relevant to the present thesis, large-scale Bayesian phylogenetic analyses of the family (Gray, Drummond & Greenhill 2009; Bouckaert et al. 2018) and Bayesian phonotactic modelling of unit discovery (Ondel et al. 2017) provide the linguistic and statistical underpinnings of the prior P_typ introduced in Chapter III. FormosanBench (Cui et al. 2025) benchmarks low-resource Austronesian languages in the era of large language models and confirms the present need for family-level transfer mechanisms. None of these works, however, constructs a phonotactic and morphotactic Austronesian prior over a shared sub-word vocabulary and incorporates it as an explicit constraint on the pseudo-label posterior of an ASR system — the contribution claimed in Component 3.2.

II.2.6 Joint dialect, register, and code-switching ASR

Each pairwise combination among dialect, register, and code-switching has been addressed in the literature. Joint dialect-conditioned ASR with a single sequence-to-sequence model was introduced by Li, Sainath et al. (2018); subsequent work includes VoxArabica (Waheed et al. 2023), DialectMoE (Yu et al. 2024), GLoRIA gated low-rank adaptation (Mundnich et al. 2026), and dedicated work on Swiss German (Khosravani et al. 2021). Joint code-switching and ASR with explicit factorization was formalized by Yan et al. (2021) as p(y_bilingual) = f(p(y_lang1), p(y_lang2)); Kulkarni et al. (2023) model the code-switching identity as a per-frame latent binary sequence that gates the flow of information through language-specific adapters — the closest published precedent for the q_c factor of Component 3.4. The intersection of dialect and code-switching is treated in the multilingual Arabic system of Chowdhury et al. (2021). Language-routing mixtures of experts have been proposed for multilingual and code-switching ASR (Wang/Kong et al. 2023; Zhao et al. 2024). Disentangled latent-variable speech models (the factorised hierarchical VAE of Hsu, Zhang & Glass 2017; Hsu & Glass 2018) and factorised speaker-environment adaptive training (2023) are conceptual antecedents for the variational treatment of the latents. Register as an explicit latent variable inferred jointly with dialect and code-switching, and the three-way mean-field coordinate-ascent inference with expected adapters inside the decoding loop, are not, to our knowledge, attested in the published literature.

II.2.7 Confidence calibration for ASR and self-training

The canonical reference for feature-based confidence calibration in ASR is Yu, Li & Deng (2011), which trains a maximum-entropy calibrator on word-level and lattice features and uses the calibrated confidence to gate unsupervised data for semi-supervised acoustic-model training — the pipeline of which Component 3.5 of the present thesis is the modern, foundation-model-era extension. Modern post-hoc calibration is dominated by temperature scaling and isotonic regression (Platt 1999; Naeini, Cooper & Hauskrecht 2015; Guo et al. 2017), evaluated by the Expected Calibration Error. Multi-task confidence estimation with explicit deletion modelling was proposed by Kumar et al. (2021). Fast entropy-based word-level confidence for end-to-end ASR was introduced by Laptev et al. (2023). Recent work has adapted Whisper itself as a confidence estimator (Aggarwal et al. 2025) and addressed the specific problem of identifying and calibrating overconfidence in noisy speech recognition (Huo, Zhang & Tang 2025). In the broader semi-supervised learning literature, FixMatch (Sohn et al. 2020), FlexMatch (Zhang et al. 2021) and FreeMatch (Wang et al. 2023) supply the canonical confidence-threshold and curriculum-thresholding mechanisms that the present work generalizes to a learned, linguistically-informed calibrator feeding both a router and a constrained-EM confidence floor.

II.2.8 The state of Malagasy and Austronesian low-resource ASR

The published literature on Malagasy ASR is, at the time of writing, exceedingly thin. VoxMg (Ramanantsoa 2023), a 10.8-hour transcribed corpus accompanied by a baseline model at approximately 33 % WER, is the single peer-reviewed contribution dedicated to Malagasy ASR. The Malagasy NLP survey of Ratianantitra (2023) treats ASR briefly, and the recent Malagasy sentiment-analysis corpus (Ratianantitra et al. 2025) is concerned with text rather than speech. A small community dataset of approximately three hours has been released by Angelina & Rabetokotany (2020). On the foundation-model side, MMS (Pratap et al. 2024) reports an aggregate average across more than one thousand languages, of which Malagasy is one, but does not publish a separately interpretable Malagasy WER on a public benchmark. AfriHuBERT (Alabi et al. 2025) continues pre-training on 1 226 African languages but does not include Malagasy in its FLEURS evaluation. The two systematic reviews of African low-resource ASR published in 2025 (Olatunji et al.; the arXiv survey 2510.01145; the benchmarking study 2512.10968) cite Malagasy at most once. To the best of the present search, no peer-reviewed WER on FLEURS-Malagasy has been published at the time of writing — itself a benchmarking gap that the empirical chapter will address.

At the level of the Austronesian family, the closest methodological cousin is the Te Reo M⁁ori work of Coto-Solano et al. (2024), which uses synthesized data selection by score-distribution matching to fine-tune Whisper-large-v3 on a single foundation model; the multilingual evaluation of Indonesian ASR by Aisyah et al. (2024) compares foundation models on dialectal variability; FormosanBench (Cui et al. 2025) is the dedicated low-resource Austronesian benchmark. None of these works deploys the heterogeneous-teacher routing and constrained variational EM architecture of the present thesis. At the regional level, Comorian work (Diarra et al. 2024 on Bambara; transfer-learning from Swahili 2024) and Mauritian Creole (Noormamode et al. 2018) are useful neighbours but not direct competitors. The ethical reflection of Mahelona et al. (2023) on the use of large Whisper-style models for indigenous languages is taken as a normative reference for the data-licensing tier of Chapter II.

Active institutional actors in Madagascar — LIAM (Laboratoire d'Intelligence Artificielle de Madagascar), IndabaX Madagascar, university groups at Antananarivo and Fianarantsoa, and emerging commercial offerings — signal that the field will not remain empty for long; the present thesis takes that prospective competition as an additional argument for publishing an explicit methodological framework rather than a single benchmark number.

II.2.3 Data construction, licensing, and reproducibility

License-first data construction has become a research contribution in its own right. The present work constructs its data substrate through a nine-stage pipeline whose outputs are partitioned into four tiers.

  • Tier A — gold supervised: professionally transcribed audio with double annotation, dialect and register labels, and a permissive license. Target volume: 200–400 hours.
  • Tier B — silver supervised: machine-assisted transcription verified by a single annotator. Target volume: 600–1 000 hours.
  • Tier C — licensed unlabeled: audio collected under licenses that permit derivative model training, without transcripts. Target volume: 10 000–30 000 hours.
  • Tier D — restricted: data whose license requires explicit, per-use authorization. Used only with explicit consent.

Each stage of the pipeline produces machine-readable manifests, persistent identifiers for each segment, and provenance metadata sufficient to reconstruct the corpus from public sources. Datasheets, model cards, and a Zenodo-archived DOI accompany every release. The data substrate is treated, in the methodology of Chapter III, as a fixed input rather than as a degree of freedom of the modeling procedure.

OPEN PROBLEMS

II.3 The four open methodological problems

Several problems are well established at thesis scale and would not, in themselves, constitute a methodological contribution: continued self-supervised pre-training for a single low-resource language; pseudo-labeling with simple confidence filtering; LoRA cross-lingual fine-tuning; dialect-conditioned adapters; code-switched ASR with a language-identification head. Applying any of these to Malagasy would be linguistically informative but methodologically incremental.

The following four problems, by contrast, remain open at thesis scale and structure the methodology of Chapter III.

  • P1. The principled probabilistic integration of multiple heterogeneous foundation models, treated as distinct posteriors and exploiting their disagreement structure as a routing signal rather than as noise to be averaged away.
  • P2. The injection of typological priors from a known language family as Bayesian priors that constrain the decoding hypothesis space where a target-language-only language model cannot.
  • P3. The formal treatment of iterative pseudo-labeling as a constrained variational EM procedure with explicit non-collapse conditions and a convergence analysis under stated simplifying assumptions.
  • P4. The unification of dialect, register, and code-switching as latent variables in a single graphical model with explicit conditional independence structure and a joint approximate inference procedure.

To these four problems is added a transversal requirement, P5, that the confidences consumed by every downstream constraint be calibrated and that the calibration generalize from a small supervised set to a larger, distributionally shifted unlabeled set.

POSITIONING

II.4 Closest prior art and the position of PROVA-MG

The present section makes explicit, for each of the five concerns identified above, the closest published work and the increment claimed by the methodology of Chapter III. The intent is to be honest about lineage: every component of PROVA-MG has identifiable antecedents, and its novelty lies in their integration and in specific technical additions, not in the invention of a wholly new framework.

  • P1 / Component 3.1 — heterogeneous co-inference. Closest precedents: Gitman et al. (2023, confidence-based ensembles), Kulkarni et al. (2024, Pratinidhi), Carofilis et al. (2025), Prakash et al. (2025), Rangappa et al. (2025). PROVA-MG extends this lineage by (i) treating Whisper-large-v3, MMS, and Wav2Vec2-BERT as three posteriors within a single probabilistic framework, (ii) replacing the heuristic argmax with a learned gradient-boosted router, (iii) producing four routing outcomes (high-confidence training, human review, reserve, discard) rather than a single keep/discard decision, and (iv) using Jensen-Shannon divergence over a shared lattice as a primary disagreement feature.
  • P2 / Component 3.2 — typological prior. Closest precedents: Klakow (1998) and Kannan et al. (2018) for log-linear LM fusion; Chan et al. (2025) for typologically aware rescoring; Khare et al. (2024) for related-language LM rescoring; Adams et al. (2019) and Adilazuarda et al. (2024) for typology-aware multilingual transfer. PROVA-MG extends this lineage by constructing an Austronesian phonotactic and morphotactic prior P_typ over a shared sub-word vocabulary (Indonesian + Malay + Cebuano + Tagalog + Malagasy) and embedding it as an explicit expectation constraint (C4) on the pseudo-label posterior of an iterative EM. To the best of the present search, no published work has built such a prior for Malagasy or used a family-level phonotactic prior as a pseudo-label gate in ASR.
  • P3 / Component 3.3 — constrained variational EM. Closest precedents: Posterior Regularization (Ganchev et al. 2010), Generalized Expectation Criteria (Mann & McCallum 2008, 2010), Alternating Projections (Bellare et al. 2009), and Unified EM (Samdani et al. 2012); empirically, the soft-label collapse analysis of Likhomanenko, Lugosch & Collobert (2023). PROVA-MG is an explicit instantiation of posterior regularization for iterative ASR pseudo-labeling; the claimed increment is (i) the integrated four-constraint set C1 (calibrated confidence floor) + C2 (between-iteration KL drift) + C3 (multi-teacher agreement) + C4 (typological consistency), (ii) the between-iteration KL drift bound C2 which is not part of the classical PR/GE formulation, and (iii) a non-collapse argument tailored to the iterative pseudo-labeling regime in the spirit of the recent iterative-MLE stability results of Bertrand et al. (2024) and Aubin et al. (2025). The thesis explicitly disclaims any reinvention of the constrained-E-step framework itself and positions Component 3.3 as its principled extension to the foundation-model ASR setting.
  • P4 / Component 3.4 — latent decomposition. Closest precedents: Yan et al. (2021) for joint code-switching factorization; Kulkarni et al. (2023) for code-switching as a latent binary sequence routing language adapters; Chowdhury et al. (2021) for joint dialect and code-switching Arabic ASR; Li, Sainath et al. (2018) for dialect-conditioned end-to-end ASR; the disentangled latent-variable speech models of Hsu, Zhang & Glass (2017). PROVA-MG extends this lineage by including register as an explicit latent jointly inferred with dialect and code-switching, by formalizing the joint as a graphical model with a mean-field variational posterior, and by performing coordinate-ascent updates with expected dialect and register adapters inside the decoding loop. The three-way (d, r, c) joint latent factorization for ASR has not, to our knowledge, been published.
  • P5 / Component 3.5 — calibration. Closest precedent: Yu, Li & Deng (2011), which is the canonical feature-based ASR calibration paper and itself uses calibrated confidences to gate semi-supervised data. PROVA-MG extends this lineage by (i) replacing the maximum-entropy classifier with a modern post-hoc calibrator (temperature, isotonic, or gradient-boosted), (ii) introducing typological and dialectal features drawn from Components 3.2 and 3.4, (iii) piping the calibrated confidence simultaneously into the router of 3.1 and the confidence-floor constraint C1 of 3.3.
  • Integrated framework. The closest integrated systems on multi-teacher pseudo-labeling for low-resource ASR are Pratinidhi (Kulkarni et al. 2024) and Carofilis et al. (2025); on Malagasy specifically, VoxMg (Ramanantsoa 2023) is the only published baseline. None of these integrates the five concerns of Components 3.1–3.5 within a single probabilistic system, and none applies such an integration to Malagasy or to its Austronesian sister languages.

CHAPTER CONCLUSION

Conclusion of Chapter II

The present chapter has surveyed the cross-lingual, weakly supervised, and adaptation methods that extend the four paradigms of Chapter I to low-resource and multilingual settings; it has described the license-first data substrate retained for the empirical instantiation on Malagasy; it has identified the four open methodological problems — heterogeneous co-inference, typological priors, constrained variational EM, latent-variable decomposition — together with the transversal calibration requirement; and it has positioned each of those five concerns against its closest published precedent, naming explicitly the lineages from posterior regularization, multi-ASR pseudo-labeling, typological rescoring, dialect-conditioned ASR, and feature-based confidence calibration that the framework of Chapter III extends. The methodology of Chapter III is structured around exactly those five concerns. The empirical validation of Chapter IV will test, for each of them, whether the proposed solution delivers a measurable and statistically significant improvement over the closest single-component baseline, and will report the result whether positive or negative.

Chapter III — The PROVA-MG Methodology

PROVA-MG / Chapter III of IV

Chapter III: The PROVA-MG Methodology

PROVA-MG — Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy — is formulated as a latent-variable probabilistic system that aggregates heterogeneous evidence under explicit calibration and explicit constraints. The present chapter derives the framework, specifies its five components and their algorithmic implementation, analyses their complexity, and describes their integration with the license-first data pipeline.

CHAPTER INTRODUCTION

A latent-variable reading of low-resource ASR

Low-resource ASR is treated, in the present work, not as a single model trained on a single objective with a single source of supervision, but as a probabilistic system that aggregates heterogeneous evidence. The substrate of that system is a graphical model in which the transcript y is jointly generated with several latent variables — dialect d, register r, code-switching identity c — conditioning the acoustic emission and the language-model prior. The estimation procedure is a constrained variational EM whose constraints are derived from the agreement of heterogeneous teachers, from a calibrated confidence head, and from a typological prior trained on the Austronesian family.

The chapter is organized in three parts. Part III.1 derives the theoretical formulation of the system: graphical structure, likelihood, prior, posterior approximation, and learning objective. Part III.2 specifies the five interlocking components in algorithmic form, with derivations, pseudocode, and complexity analysis. Part III.3 describes the training protocol, the optimization schedule, and the integration with the data pipeline of Chapter II.

PART THREE — A

III.1 Theoretical formulation

III.1.1 The generative model

Let x denote the acoustic signal and y the transcript. The latent variables of the system are d (dialect, categorical with K_d levels), r (register, categorical with K_r levels, distinguishing read, broadcast, conversational, and ceremonial speech), and c (per-segment code-switching identity, taking values in {MG, FR, mixed}). The generative model factorizes as

p(x, y, d, r, c) = p(d) p(r) p(c | r, d) p(y | d, r, c) p(x | y, d, r)

which encodes three modelling decisions. The dialect and register are marginally independent, reflecting the empirical observation that a Merina speaker can be recorded in either a read or a conversational register. The code-switching identity is conditioned on register and dialect because code-switching is itself sociolinguistically structured. The acoustic emission depends on the transcript, the dialect, and the register, but not on the code-switching identity beyond what is already encoded in the transcript and the dialect.

III.1.2 The variational posterior

Exact inference under the model above is intractable. A mean-field variational posterior is therefore introduced:

q(y, d, r, c | x) = q_y(y | x) q_d(d | x) qᵣ(r | x) q_c(c | x, y)

Each factor of q is parameterized by a neural network. The factor q_y is the transcript posterior of an ASR head; the factors q_d and qᵣ are classification heads predicting dialect and register from the acoustic input; the factor q_c is a sequence labeller predicting code-switching identity per segment of the transcript. The mean-field factorization is admissible because the model decouples d, r, and c at the prior level; residual dependence is captured by the conditioning of every factor on x.

III.1.3 The evidence lower bound

The learning objective is the standard evidence lower bound (ELBO) on the marginal log-likelihood of the observed data:

log p(x, y) ≥ L_(ELBO)(θ, φ) = E_q[ log p_θ(x, y, d, r, c) ] - E_q[ log q_φ(y, d, r, c | x) ] = E_q[ log p_θ(x | y, d, r) p_θ(y | d, r, c) ] - KL( q_φ ‖ p )

where θ parameterizes the generative model and φ the variational posterior. On the supervised subset of the data the transcript y is observed and the corresponding factor of q is replaced by a delta on the gold transcript; on the unsupervised subset y is latent and the variational posterior is unrolled jointly with the other latent factors.

III.1.4 The constrained variational EM

On the union of the supervised and unsupervised subsets the parameters θ and the variational posterior q are estimated jointly by an EM procedure. The E-step minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between q and p_θ( · | x) subject to a constraint set C; the M-step maximizes the expected complete-data log-likelihood plus a parameter regularizer:

E-step: q^* = argmin_(q ∈ C) KL( q ‖ p_θ( · | x) ) M-step: θ ← argmax_θ E_(q^*)[ log p_θ(x, y, d, r, c) ] + λ R(θ)

The constraint set C is the locus of the methodological contribution. It comprises four constraints, each derived from one of the open problems identified in Chapter II.

III.1.5 The four constraints

  • C1 — confidence floor. Pseudo-labels are admitted only above a calibrated confidence threshold τ: q^*(y | x) is supported only on transcripts with conf_(cal)(y, x) ≥ τ.
  • C2 — KL drift bound. Across successive iterations n and n+1, the variational posterior is constrained to drift slowly: Eₓ[ KL( q^((n+1)) ‖ q^((n)) ) ] ≤ ε.
  • C3 — teacher agreement. The support of q^* intersects the n-best lists of at least two of the three teachers of Component 3.1.
  • C4 — typological consistency. The expected typological log-likelihood under q^* is bounded below: E_(q^*)[ log P_(typ)(y) ] ≥ -η.

KL drift bound (C2): Eₓ[ KL( q^((n+1))( · | x) ‖ q^((n))( · | x) ) ] ≤ ε

Under the four constraints, the E-step is a constrained optimization that admits, in the discrete-support case, a projected-gradient or barrier-method implementation; the M-step retains its standard gradient form on θ. A short convergence argument (Section III.3) shows that under C1-C4 the iteration cannot exhibit the runaway collapse characteristic of unconstrained pseudo-labeling.

PART THREE — B

III.2 The five components

The theoretical formulation of Part III.1 is instantiated by five interlocking components. Each is specified below with its derivation, its pseudocode, and a complexity analysis.

ALGORITHM 3.1 — CO-INFERENCE ROUTING

Component 3.1

Heterogeneous foundation-model co-inference

Whisper-large-v3, MMS, and Wav2Vec2-BERT are treated as three approximate posteriors over the transcript rather than as competing baselines. Each model encodes a different inductive bias (weak supervision, religious-text alignment, self-supervision); their disagreement on a given Malagasy segment is therefore informative. For each unlabeled segment x, the approximate posteriors q_W(y | x), q_M(y | x), q_B(y | x) are computed in n-best form and a learned routing function is defined:

r : ( q_W(y | x), q_M(y | x), q_B(y | x) ) → { train_high_confidence, route_to_human, hold_in_reserve, discard }

The features consumed by r include: per-teacher top-1 confidence (calibrated), n-best overlap between teachers, pairwise edit distance between top-1 transcripts, posterior entropy of each teacher, length agreement, and the Jensen-Shannon divergence between teacher posterior distributions over a shared lattice. The routing function is trained as a gradient-boosted classifier on the supervised set, with the four routing outcomes as targets supplied by the agreement of each teacher's top-1 with the gold transcript.

for each unlabeled segment x:

  q_W ← whisper_large_v3.posterior(x)

  q_M ← mms.posterior(x)

  q_B ← wav2vec2_bert.posterior(x)

  f ← features(q_W, q_M, q_B)

  decision ← r(f)

  if decision == train_high_confidence:

    yhat ← consensus_decode(q_W, q_M, q_B)

    emit (x, yhat, conf_cal)

  elif decision == route_to_human:

    queue.enqueue(x, q_W, q_M, q_B)

  elif decision == hold_in_reserve:

    reserve.put(x, features=f)

  else:

    discard(x)

Complexity. The dominant cost is the three forward passes through the foundation models. Let n denote the number of segments and T the mean segment length in frames. Inference is O(n T (d_W + d_M + d_B)), where d_* is the model dimension. Feature extraction and routing add O(n B^2) where B is the n-best width. The routing classifier itself is sub-linear in n. The dominant memory cost is the storage of the three posteriors, mitigated by retaining only the top-B paths.

ALGORITHM 3.2 — TYPOLOGICAL PRIOR INTEGRATION

Component 3.2

Typologically informed Bayesian priors

Malagasy belongs to the Malayo-Polynesian subgroup. Its phonotactics and morphology overlap measurably with Indonesian, Malay, Cebuano, and Tagalog, all of which have substantially larger text corpora. A phonotactic and morphotactic prior P_(typ) is trained on Austronesian text and incorporated into decoding through a calibrated log-linear mixture:

log P(y | x) ∝ log P_(acoustic)(x | y) + α log P_(LM-MG)(y) + β log P_(typ)(y)

The hyperparameters α and β are tuned on the development set by grid search subject to the constraint that the mixture remains a valid log-posterior (positive weights summing to a fixed total). P_(typ) is implemented as a sub-word language model over a shared phonotactic vocabulary; transfer to Malagasy proceeds through a morphological mapping that aligns Austronesian affixes to their Malagasy cognates.

# Training of P_typ

corpus ← Indonesian + Malay + Cebuano + Tagalog + Malagasy (text)

vocab ← shared_BPE(corpus, size=8000)

P_typ ← train_LM(vocab, corpus)

# Decoding

for each beam hypothesis y in beam_search:

  s_acoustic ← log P_acoustic(x | y)

  s_LM ← alpha * log P_LM_MG(y)

  s_typ ← beta * log P_typ(y)

  score(y) ← s_acoustic + s_LM + s_typ

Complexity. The prior is evaluated during beam search, adding O(B T |V|) to the decoding cost, where |V| is the vocabulary size and B the beam width. The cost is amortized by caching the language-model state across beam expansions.

ALGORITHM 3.3 — CONSTRAINED VARIATIONAL EM

Component 3.3

Constrained variational EM for iterative pseudo-labeling

On the extended dataset D = Dₛᵤₚ ∪ Dᵤₙₛᵤₚ, parameters θ and latent transcripts are inferred jointly through the constrained EM derived in Part III.1. The four constraints C1–C4 act on the E-step support.

E-step: q^*(y | x) = argmin_(q ∈ C) KL( q ‖ p_θ(y | x) ) M-step: θ ← argmax_θ E_(q^*)[ log p_θ(yₛᵤₚ, yᵤₙₛᵤₚ, x) ] + λ R(θ)

theta ← init_from_supervised(D_sup)

for iteration n = 1, ..., N:

  # E-step (per segment)

  for each x in D_unsup:

    n_best ← decode_top_B(theta, x)

    n_best ← filter_by_confidence(n_best, tau) # C1

    n_best ← intersect_with_teachers(n_best, q_W, q_M, q_B) # C3

    n_best ← filter_by_typology(n_best, P_typ, eta) # C4

    q_star(. | x) ← renormalize(n_best)

    assert KL(q_star || q_prev[x]) ≤ epsilon # C2

  # M-step

  theta ← sgd_step(D_sup ∪ {(x, q_star) : x in D_unsup})

  q_prev ← q_star

  if held_out_loss(theta) - prev_loss > delta: break

Non-collapse argument. Without constraints, iterative pseudo-labeling can exhibit confidence inflation accompanied by accuracy degradation — the canonical collapse mode. Under C1 (confidence floor on calibrated confidence) the support of q^* cannot expand into low-confidence regions; under C2 (KL drift bound) the variational posterior cannot move arbitrarily fast across iterations; under C3 (teacher agreement) the support is intersected with the union of teacher n-best lists, which by construction reflects independent inductive biases; under C4 (typological consistency) the support is pruned of transcripts that violate Austronesian phonotactics. The intersection of these four constraints bounds the iterative drift in both confidence space and hypothesis space.

Complexity. Each EM iteration is O(|Dᵤₙₛᵤₚ| (decoding + feature extraction)) in the E-step and O(|D| epochs) in the M-step. The total cost is N times that of a single fine-tuning run, with N typically between three and six.

ALGORITHM 3.4 — JOINT MEAN-FIELD INFERENCE

Component 3.4

Latent-variable decomposition: dialect, register, code-switching

The graphical model of Part III.1 makes dialect, register, and code-switching latent variables jointly inferred with the transcript. The acoustic model factorizes as p(x | y, d, r) and the language model as p(y | d, c, r). Dialect-specific adapters condition on d, register-specific parameters on r, and code-switched segments are routed through a French acoustic model.

x → ( d, r, c, y ) d = dialect (Merina, Betsimisaraka, Sakalava, Antandroy, …) r = register (read, broadcast, conversational, ceremonial) c = per-segment code-switching identity (MG, FR, mixed)

Approximate inference proceeds by mean-field updates: each factor q_d, qᵣ, q_c is updated holding the others fixed, and the transcript factor q_y is updated by decoding with the current expected dialect and register adapters.

init q_d, q_r, q_c, q_y from heads

repeat until convergence:

  q_d ← softmax( log p(d) + E_{q_r,q_c,q_y}[ log p(x,y,d,r,c) ] )

  q_r ← softmax( log p(r) + E_{q_d,q_c,q_y}[ log p(x,y,d,r,c) ] )

  q_c ← softmax( log p(c|r,d) + E_{q_d,q_r,q_y}[ log p(y,c) ] )

  q_y ← decode_with_adapters( E_{q_d}[adapter_d], E_{q_r}[adapter_r], x )

Complexity. The dominant cost is the repeated decoding inside the loop. In practice, two to three coordinate-ascent passes suffice for convergence; total cost is O(I T (encoder + decoder)) where I is the number of passes.

ALGORITHM 3.5 — CALIBRATION TRAINING AND USE

Component 3.5

Linguistically informed confidence calibration

ASR models are typically over-confident, and miscalibrated confidences would compromise both the routing of Component 3.1 and the constraints of Component 3.3. A post-hoc calibration model is therefore trained on the supervised set.

Calibrated probability: p_(cal)(correct | features) = g_φ(features)

where g_φ is implemented either as temperature scaling (single parameter) or as isotonic regression (non-parametric) or as a small gradient-boosted classifier on the feature set. The features are: per-teacher posterior entropy, three-way teacher agreement, typological log-likelihood, segment duration, voice-activity confidence, dialect-posterior entropy, and the rank of the top-1 hypothesis in the consensus lattice. The calibration objective is the negative log-likelihood on the supervised set plus a smoothness penalty:

L_(cal)(φ) = -∑_((x,y) ∈ Dₛᵤₚ) log g_φ( features(x), 1[ ŷ(x) = y ] ) + μ ‖ g_φ ‖²

The calibration quality is measured by the Expected Calibration Error with n bins:

ECEₙ = ∑_b (|B_b|)/N | acc(B_b) - conf(B_b) |

# Training

features ← extract(D_sup, teachers, P_typ)

targets ← 1[ yhat == y ] for (x, y) in D_sup

phi ← fit_calibrator(features, targets)

# Use

conf_cal ← g_phi( extract(x, teachers, P_typ) )

Complexity. Calibration training is linear in |Dₛᵤₚ|. Use at inference is O(1) per segment after feature extraction.

UNIFYING CLAIM — The calibrated confidence (Component 3.5) feeds the routing of 3.1 and the constraints of 3.3; the typological prior (3.2) feeds the constraint C4; the teacher agreement of 3.1 feeds the constraint C3; the latent decomposition of 3.4 feeds the conditional adapters consumed by every other component. The framework is therefore not a list of independent techniques but a system whose components reinforce one another.

PART THREE — C

III.3 Training protocol and integration with the data pipeline

III.3.1 Stage 1 — Initialization from supervised set

The acoustic head is initialized by fine-tuning Wav2Vec2-BERT on the Tier-A supervised set with a CTC objective and LoRA adapters of rank 16. The dialect, register, and code-switching heads are trained jointly on the same supervised set, supervised by the available metadata labels.

III.3.2 Stage 2 — Teacher inference on unlabeled pool

The three teachers are run on Tier-C unlabeled data. The output is stored as compressed n-best lattices with per-path posterior scores. This stage is embarrassingly parallel and dominates the compute budget; on the target hardware it requires of the order of one GPU-week per 10 000 hours of audio.

III.3.3 Stage 3 — Routing and calibration

The routing function and the calibration head are trained on the supervised set with features extracted from the Stage-2 teacher outputs. The calibrator is then evaluated for distribution shift between the supervised and the unlabeled pool by a held-out reliability diagram.

III.3.4 Stage 4 — Constrained EM loop

The constrained EM loop of Component 3.3 is executed for between three and six iterations, with each iteration consuming the Stage-2 teacher outputs and producing an updated θ. The loop terminates either when held-out loss stops improving or when the KL drift bound saturates.

III.3.5 Stage 5 — Joint latent inference and final evaluation

The final model performs joint mean-field inference over dialect, register, code-switching, and transcript on the frozen test sets. Stratified evaluation is then conducted across all three test sets and all four dialect strata.

III.3.6 Optimization details

Optimization uses AdamW with a cosine schedule, peak learning rate 3e-5 for the LoRA adapters and 1e-4 for the heads, batch size 16 with gradient accumulation to an effective 64, dropout 0.1 in the adapters and 0.0 in the frozen backbone, label smoothing 0.1 for attention-based decoders, mixed-precision (bf16) on the target hardware, gradient clipping at 1.0, and a small auxiliary CTC loss in joint CTC-attention runs with weight 0.3.

CHAPTER CONCLUSION

Conclusion of Chapter III

The present chapter has formulated PROVA-MG as a latent-variable probabilistic system; specified its five components — co-inference, typological prior, constrained variational EM, latent decomposition, calibration — in algorithmic form with derivations and complexity analyses; and described a five-stage training protocol that integrates the framework with the license-first data pipeline of Chapter II. The next chapter presents the prototype implementation, the experimental matrix, the expected results, the discussion of limitations, and the perspectives of further work.
