Chapter IV: Application, Results and Discussion

The present chapter describes the prototype implementation of PROVA-MG, presents the experimental matrix in placeholder form pending the experimental run, discusses the expected results and their limitations, situates the framework with respect to the closest prior art, lays out the publication plan, the eight-phase validation procedure with measurable gates, and the perspectives of further work.

CHAPTER INTRODUCTION

From methodology to evidence

The framework specified in Chapter III is, at the moment of writing, instantiated in a prototype implementation whose components have been brought separately to functional readiness and whose integration is under way. The present chapter is organized in four substantive parts plus the validation plan inherited from earlier drafts. Part IV.1 describes the prototype: software stack, model registry, infrastructure. Part IV.2 lays out the experimental matrix in placeholder form, with full headers and labels so that, on each completed experiment, the corresponding cell is to be filled. Part IV.3 discusses the expected interpretation patterns, limitations beyond the existing list, and threats to validity. Part IV.4 develops the perspectives of further work, deployment, ethics, and dialect equity. The publication plan, the positioning with respect to prior art, and the eight-phase validation procedure are then preserved in their earlier form.

PART FOUR — A

IV.1 Application: prototype implementation

IV.1.1 Software stack

The prototype is built in Python 3.11 on top of the PyTorch 2.x runtime. Data loading and tokenization go through the Hugging Face datasets and transformers libraries; foundation model inference uses transformers and, for Whisper, optionally the faster-whisper port of CTranslate2. Training uses accelerate for distributed orchestration and peft for LoRA adapter management. Evaluation uses jiwer for WER and CER, scipy for paired bootstrap and Wilcoxon tests, and scikit-learn for calibration (temperature scaling and isotonic regression). Experiment tracking goes through Weights & Biases with offline fallback to a local SQLite store; every run logs the pinned environment hash and the seed.

IV.1.2 Model registry

A local model registry — a versioned directory tree with a JSON index — holds, for each foundation model and each fine-tuned variant: the weights (or a pointer to the public checkpoint), the configuration, the tokenizer, the model card, and the training manifest. Three foundation checkpoints are registered as teachers; subsequent fine-tuned variants are tagged with the upstream commit hash of the configuration and the data manifest version on which they were trained.

IV.1.3 Infrastructure

Training and inference run on a small heterogeneous cluster comprising consumer-grade and server-grade GPUs (A100-80GB, A40, RTX-4090-class), with mixed-precision (bf16) where supported and fp16 elsewhere. Long inference passes on the Tier-C unlabeled pool are sharded across nodes and the resulting n-best lattices are compressed and stored on shared object storage. A reproducible Docker image, archived with its hash, packages the runtime environment.

PART FOUR — C

IV.3 Discussion: expected patterns, limitations, threats to validity

IV.3.1 Expected interpretation patterns

Under the working hypotheses of the General Introduction, four interpretation patterns are anticipated. First, the gain of routing over averaging is expected to concentrate on segments of intermediate teacher agreement: where all three teachers agree, averaging and routing coincide; where teachers disagree strongly, routing should defer to human review rather than commit to a likely-wrong consensus. Second, the typological prior is expected to act selectively on low-frequency morphology and on rare segmental sequences, with little effect on high-frequency lexical items already well covered by the Malagasy language model. Third, the constrained EM is expected to improve held-out WER monotonically across iterations under the full constraint set, and to exhibit clear divergence under the constraint-ablated runs. Fourth, the joint latent inference is expected to improve performance on under-represented dialects (Betsimisaraka, Sakalava, Antandroy) without degradation on Merina, and to handle code-switched segments better than a single Malagasy-only system.

IV.3.2 Limitations beyond the existing list

Several limitations condition the interpretation of the expected results beyond those listed in Part IV.D below.

  • Dialect category granularity. The four-way dialect partition (Merina, Betsimisaraka, Sakalava, Antandroy) is a simplification: at least eighteen dialect groups are recognized linguistically, and several of the four groups are themselves internally heterogeneous. The latent variable d is therefore coarser than the linguistic reality.
  • Calibration set size. The supervised set on which the calibrator is fit is, in absolute terms, small. The distribution-shift study of Phase 3 is intended to detect calibration breakdown, but it cannot in itself prevent it.
  • Anchoring bias in correction. Tier-B annotators see the seed transcription before correcting it, which is known to introduce an anchoring bias toward the seed. A double-annotation sample is therefore retained on which the bias is measured and reported.
  • Compute-limited iteration count. The constrained EM is in principle iterated until convergence; in practice the iteration count is bounded by available compute. A budget of six iterations is planned and reported as a hyperparameter rather than as a converged result.
  • Speech-LLM comparisons. Speech-LLMs are not on the load-bearing path; a comparison may therefore not be available at the date of defense and is recorded as a future work item.

IV.3.3 Threats to validity

Four threats to validity are identified at the methodological level. Construct validity: WER and CER are imperfect proxies for downstream task quality; a small qualitative evaluation on transcripts intended for accessibility and educational applications is therefore retained. Internal validity: the integration of five interacting components creates a risk of confounding between component effects; the leave-one-out ablation of Table 4.2 is designed precisely to bound that risk, complemented by selected leave-two-out runs on the components whose interaction is theoretically expected to be largest. External validity: the methodology is instantiated on Malagasy; its transfer to other low-resource Austronesian languages (Tagalog with its own resource gradient, Cebuano, the languages of eastern Indonesia) is a future work item, not a claim of the present thesis. Conclusion validity: significance tests across the full matrix invite multiple-comparison inflation; Bonferroni correction is applied to the family of headline comparisons.

IV.3.4 Comparison to prior numbers in the literature

Published numbers for Malagasy ASR are sparse and use heterogeneous test sets. Whisper-large-v3 zero-shot WER on FLEURS-MG has been reported around the high-forties; MMS fine-tuned on Common Voice-MG has been reported in the low-thirties; XLS-R fine-tuned on Common Voice-MG has appeared in the high-twenties on the same test set. The thesis targets — at or below 15% WER on read speech and at or below 25% WER on spontaneous speech — are therefore ambitious relative to the published state of the art, and their attainment, if confirmed, would constitute a substantive empirical contribution in addition to the methodological one.

PART FOUR — D

IV.4 Perspectives: future work, deployment, ethics, dialect equity

IV.4.1 Future technical work

Several technical extensions are envisaged beyond the scope of the present thesis. Speech-LLM integration: a comparison and possibly an integration of the PROVA-MG output with a speech-LLM as a downstream rescorer. On-device deployment: distillation of the integrated framework into a compact (sub-100M-parameter) student suitable for inference on mobile hardware. Streaming variant: replacement of the offline encoder by a streaming Conformer with chunked attention, enabling real-time transcription. Cross-lingual transfer: instantiation of the framework on another low-resource Austronesian language to test the generality of the typological prior.

IV.4.2 Deployment and applications

A small set of applications is identified as priority deployment targets, conditional on the attainment of the WER thresholds. Educational support tools transcribe classroom audio for review by pupils and teachers, with manual correction as a learning activity. Accessibility services produce captions for live broadcast and recorded media. Administrative transcription accelerates the conversion of public-hearing audio into searchable text. Journalistic indexing produces searchable transcripts of interview archives. Each application requires a domain-specific qualitative evaluation and a written consent regime appropriate to the recording setting.

IV.4.3 Ethics

Three ethical considerations are integrated into the design. Consent and licensing: every recording entering the corpus is accompanied by a verifiable consent and license document, and Tier-D recordings are excluded from any open release. Speaker privacy: voice models pose a potential re-identification risk; the published student model is therefore distilled from a teacher trained on a privacy-screened subset, and a model card discloses the residual risk. Use restriction: model cards explicitly disallow surveillance applications and require the propagation of the use restriction in any derivative work.

IV.4.4 Dialect equity

Dialect equity is treated as an evaluation dimension rather than as a secondary concern. The stratified evaluation of Table 4.7 reports per-dialect WER explicitly; a deployment is considered usable only when the worst-dialect WER is within a stated factor of the best-dialect WER. The factor is conservatively set to two for the present thesis and is intended to tighten as the corpus expands.

PART FOUR — A

Positioning with respect to prior art

Each component of PROVA-MG draws on existing literature; the contribution lies in the specific formulation of each component and in their integration. The following table summarizes the nearest prior art and the elements that are new in the present work.

ComponentNearest prior artContribution of the present work
3.1 Co-inferenceEnsemble distillation, DistilWhisperTeachers treated as distinct posteriors with informative disagreement; routing rather than averaging.
3.2 Typological priorsLanguage-family adapters in low-resource machine translationExplicit Bayesian prior on phonotactics integrated into the decoding probability.
3.3 Constrained EMslimIPL, Kaizen, Noisy Student TrainingFormal convergence and non-collapse conditions in constrained variational form.
3.4 Latent decompositionDialect adapters for Arabic and ChineseJoint inference of dialect, register, and code-switching within a single generative model.
3.5 CalibrationPost-hoc calibration in classificationCalibration that generalizes from a small supervised set to a larger, distributionally shifted unlabeled set.

The integration of the five components is itself a contribution: the calibrated confidence (3.5), the agreement signal (3.1), and the constraint set (3.3) are shared across components, so that they reinforce one another rather than operating in isolation.

Validation plan: phases, tasks, and gates

The validation procedure is decomposed into eight phases. Each phase terminates with a gate, a measurable result that must hold before the next phase begins. Items can be marked as they are completed; progress is persisted automatically.

P0

Foundations, infrastructure, and evaluation harness

A reliable measuring instrument is the precondition for every subsequent phase.

P0.1 Consolidate the literature review into a single internal document mapping every PROVA-MG component to its nearest prior art. — Deliverable: state-of-the-art chapter draft.

P0.2 Set up the reproducible compute environment (Python 3.10+, PyTorch, Transformers, Datasets, Accelerate) and archive it as a versioned Docker image. — Deliverable: pinned environment and image hash.

P0.3 Build the evaluation harness: WER and CER with jiwer, plus paired bootstrap, MAPSSWE, and Wilcoxon significance tests. — Deliverable: a single command produces a metrics report with confidence intervals.

P0.4 Define and freeze the held-out test sets: FLEURS-MG, Common Voice-MG, and a speaker-disjoint in-domain split, each stratified by dialect and register. — Deliverable: frozen test manifests, untouched during development.

P0.5 Reproduce published baselines: zero-shot Whisper-large-v3, XLS-R fine-tuned, MMS, on FLEURS-MG and CV-MG. — Deliverable: baseline WER table consistent with public numbers.

P0.6 Configure experiment tracking (Weights & Biases or MLflow) so that every run is logged, seeded, and reproducible. — Deliverable: tracked-experiment template.

Gate 0   Baselines reproduce within a small margin of published WER, and the harness produces stable confidence intervals on a repeated run.

P1

Data substrate (license-first pipeline)

PROVA-MG consumes a gold supervised set and a large licensed unlabeled set; the pipeline produces both.

P1.1 Execute the pipeline end-to-end on the pilot corpus (approximately 20 h, Tier A and Tier C); verify that every one of the nine stages functions as specified. — Deliverable: pilot corpus and stage manifests.

P1.2 Onboard professional Malagasy transcribers; reach the inter-annotator CER target on double-annotated segments. — Deliverable: agreement report meeting the threshold.

P1.3 Populate the SIGUL article (Paper 1) with pilot numbers and submit it. — Deliverable: SIGUL submission.

P1.4 Scale to the intermediate corpus (approximately 200 h) covering at least three dialects, with register metadata. — Deliverable: corpus v1 on Hugging Face with datasheet.

P1.5 Scale to the full corpus (1 000+ h supervised plus the large unlabeled pool), balanced across dialect and register. — Deliverable: corpus v2, Zenodo-archived with persistent DOI.

Gate 1   A licensed unlabeled pool sufficient for pseudo-labeling exists, and the supervised set is sufficient to train a routing function and a calibration head.

P2

Component 3.1 — Heterogeneous foundation-model co-inference

Show that routing across distinct teachers outperforms any single teacher, averaging, and voting.

P2.1 Implement posterior extraction for Whisper-large-v3, MMS, and Wav2Vec2-BERT with normalized, comparable beam scores. — Deliverable: per-segment posterior dumps for the unlabeled pool.

P2.2 Engineer the agreement feature set (n-best overlap, edit distance between teachers, entropy, length agreement). — Deliverable: feature table aligned to the supervised set.

P2.3 Train the routing function on the supervised set, predicting one of the four routing outcomes. — Deliverable: trained router and held-out routing accuracy.

P2.4 Run the controlled ablation: best single teacher vs n-best voting vs posterior averaging vs PROVA-MG routing, on identical data. — Deliverable: ablation table with significance tests.

P2.5 Distill the co-inference into a single student model and verify that it retains most of the gain at deployment cost. — Deliverable: student model with cost/quality comparison.

P2.6 Write and submit Paper 2 (co-inference). — Deliverable: Interspeech or ICASSP submission.

Gate 2   Routing yields a statistically significant WER reduction over the best single teacher and over averaging, on at least two test sets. Otherwise, the disagreement signal is not informative and Component 3.1 must be revised.

P3

Component 3.5 — Confidence calibration

Built early because both 3.1 routing and 3.3 constraints consume calibrated confidence.

P3.1 Extract calibration features (model entropy, three-way agreement, typological likelihood, duration, VAD confidence, dialect-posterior entropy). — Deliverable: calibration feature pipeline.

P3.2 Train the post-hoc calibration model (temperature scaling and isotonic regression) on the supervised set. — Deliverable: fitted calibrator.

P3.3 Measure calibration with reliability diagrams and Expected Calibration Error before and after fitting. — Deliverable: ECE table and reliability plots.

P3.4 Run the distribution-shift study: does a calibrator fit on the small supervised set still calibrate the larger, shifted unlabeled pool? — Deliverable: shift-robustness analysis.

P3.5 Ablation: re-run 3.1 routing with raw vs calibrated confidence and quantify the difference. — Deliverable: calibrated-vs-uncalibrated routing table.

Gate 3   Calibrated confidence has substantially lower ECE than raw confidence and improves routing decisions; the calibrator generalizes from the supervised set to the unlabeled distribution.

P4

Component 3.2 — Typologically informed priors

Show that an Austronesian family prior constrains decoding where a Malagasy-only language model cannot.

P4.1 Collect and clean Austronesian text corpora (Indonesian, Malay, Cebuano, Tagalog) together with all available Malagasy text. — Deliverable: family text corpus with provenance.

P4.2 Train the phonotactic and morphotactic prior P_typ on the family corpus. — Deliverable: trained typological prior model.

P4.3 Integrate the prior into decoding through the calibrated mixture; tune the mixture weights on the development set. — Deliverable: decoder with tuned weights.

P4.4 Ablation: decode with no prior vs Malagasy-only LM vs Malagasy LM combined with the typological prior. — Deliverable: prior ablation table.

P4.5 Error-localization study: verify that any gain concentrates on sparse-data regions (rare morphology, low-frequency words) rather than uniformly. — Deliverable: stratified error analysis.

P4.6 Write and submit Paper 3 (typological priors). A negative result is reported and submitted. — Deliverable: ACL or EMNLP submission.

Gate 4   Either the typological prior produces a measurable, localized WER gain (component confirmed), or it does not (component recorded as a documented negative result and dropped from the load-bearing path).

P5

Component 3.3 — Constrained variational EM

The theoretically heaviest component. Establish convergence, non-collapse, and the contribution of each constraint.

P5.1 Write the formal specification of the E-step, M-step, and the four constraints (confidence floor, KL drift bound, agreement, typological consistency). — Deliverable: formal methodology section.

P5.2 Derive convergence to a stationary point under stated simplifying assumptions. — Deliverable: proof (or proof sketch) with explicit assumptions.

P5.3 Implement the iterative loop with all constraints toggleable independently. — Deliverable: working constrained-EM trainer.

P5.4 Run the loop and plot empirical convergence: WER and held-out loss across iterations. — Deliverable: convergence curves.

P5.5 Deliberately induce model collapse with constraints disabled, and show that constraints enabled prevent it (confidence rising while accuracy falls vs both remaining aligned). — Deliverable: collapse-vs-no-collapse comparison.

P5.6 Leave-one-constraint-out ablation: quantify the contribution of each of the four constraints. — Deliverable: constraint ablation table.

P5.7 Write and submit Paper 4 (constrained variational EM) to a journal. — Deliverable: Computer Speech and Language or TASLP submission.

Gate 5   The constrained loop improves WER monotonically (or near-monotonically) across iterations, the unconstrained loop demonstrably collapses, and each constraint has a measurable effect.

P6

Component 3.4 — Latent dialect, register, code-switching

Show that joint inference of the latent variables outperforms treating them as separate subproblems.

P6.1 Specify the graphical model and its conditional independence structure. — Deliverable: model specification.

P6.2 Implement dialect-conditioned adapters and register-conditioned decoding parameters. — Deliverable: conditioned model variants.

P6.3 Implement the per-segment code-switching head and the routing of French segments. — Deliverable: code-switching-aware decoder.

P6.4 Implement joint approximate inference (variational mean-field or sampling) over dialect, register, code-switching, and transcript. — Deliverable: joint inference routine.

P6.5 Ablation: independent per-subproblem handling vs joint latent-variable inference. — Deliverable: joint-vs-separate table.

P6.6 Stratified evaluation: WER by dialect, by register, and by code-switching density, with per-dialect equity reported explicitly. — Deliverable: stratified results table.

P6.7 Write and submit Paper 5 (joint dialect, register, code-switching and calibration). — Deliverable: Interspeech submission.

Gate 6   Joint inference reduces WER on under-represented dialects and code-switched speech without degrading the majority dialect.

P7

Full-system validation and the thesis claim

Show that the integrated system outperforms every subset of its components and every published baseline.

P7.1 Run the full PROVA-MG system end-to-end on the full corpus and report WER on all three frozen test sets. — Deliverable: headline results table.

P7.2 Run the master ablation: full system minus each component in turn, demonstrating the integration claim. — Deliverable: component-removal ablation with significance tests.

P7.3 Compare against zero-shot and naively fine-tuned baselines, and against the thesis WER targets (≤15% read, ≤25% spontaneous). — Deliverable: target-attainment table.

P7.4 Statistical significance: paired bootstrap and Wilcoxon on every headline comparison. — Deliverable: significance appendix.

P7.5 Write the Threats to Validity section: small calibration set, dialect-category simplification, anchoring bias in correction, compute limits. — Deliverable: threats-to-validity chapter.

P7.6 Release all artifacts: corpus, models, code, reproducibility bundles, datasheets, and model cards, under open licenses with a persistent DOI. — Deliverable: open release package.

P7.7 Assemble the manuscript: state of the art, formalization, data substrate, the five components, full-system validation, conclusion. — Deliverable: thesis manuscript.

P7.8 Defense preparation and final open releases. — Deliverable: defended thesis.

Gate 7 (thesis claim)   The integrated PROVA-MG system significantly outperforms every ablation and every baseline on independent, frozen, dialect-stratified test sets, and the gain is attributable to the integration rather than to any single component alone.

PART FOUR — C

Discussion: limitations and mitigations

The methodology presents several limitations that condition the interpretation of its expected results. They are listed below together with their mitigations.

  • Scope. Five components constitute an ambitious programme. A defensible minimal thesis comprises Components 3.1, 3.3, and 3.5; Components 3.2 and 3.4 may be reported as future work if time becomes insufficient.
  • Theoretical depth. Components 3.3 and 3.5 require non-trivial variational inference, EM convergence, and calibration theory. Adequate probabilistic supervision is therefore necessary; if it is unavailable, Component 3.3 is restricted to empirical claims supported by proof sketches.
  • Empirical uncertainty. The typological prior of Component 3.2 may fail to reduce WER if the Malagasy language model is sufficiently strong. The corresponding ablation is therefore essential, and a negative result is itself a publishable outcome.
  • Compute. Operating three teachers at scale is costly. Distillation of the co-inference into a single student model after corpus construction is therefore planned; teachers are required at training time but not at deployment.
  • Priority of novelty. Early publication is preferred. The SIGUL submission anchors priority on the data substrate, and an early Interspeech submission on Component 3.1 anchors priority on the methodological contribution.

PROVA-MG — Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy.

Chapter 4 of 4 · Doctoral School 3D, University of Toamasina.

BACK MATTER

General Conclusion

PROVA-MG / General Conclusion

General Conclusion and Perspectives

A reminder of the topic, a recapitulation of the broad lines of the argument, a reminder of the research problem, an account of the main findings as expected, a reminder of the novelty, an acknowledgment of the limits, and a statement of the open perspectives.

REMINDER

Reminder of the topic

The present thesis was concerned with the problem of constructing an automatic speech recognition system for the Malagasy language — a low-resource Austronesian language with at least eighteen recognized dialects and a pervasive code-switching with French — under conditions that no single foundation model, supervision regime, or adaptation technique can satisfy on its own. The topic was approached as a question of methodology rather than as a question of model architecture: not which network, but which inferential framework could combine, in a principled way, the heterogeneous evidence available to a low-resource setting.

RECAPITULATION

Broad lines of the argument

Chapter I reviewed the four foundational paradigms of speech recognition — HMM-GMM, hybrid DNN-HMM, end-to-end neural, self-supervised representation — together with the mathematics that connects them, with emphasis on the elements that would re-appear in the methodology. Chapter II extended the survey to multilingual and low-resource methods, described the license-first data substrate of the present work, and identified four open methodological problems: heterogeneous co-inference, typological priors, constrained variational EM for pseudo-labeling, and latent-variable decomposition of dialect, register, and code-switching. Chapter III formulated PROVA-MG — Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy — as a latent-variable probabilistic system addressing the four problems jointly through five interlocking components, with a transversal calibration head that feeds every downstream constraint. Chapter IV described the prototype implementation, the experimental matrix, the expected interpretation patterns, the limitations, the perspectives, and the eight-phase validation procedure that operationalizes the empirical confrontation.

PROBLEM

Reminder of the research problem

The research problem was: under what conditions, and with what methodological apparatus, can the existing foundation models for multilingual speech recognition be combined with the available licensed Malagasy audio so as to yield a deployable ASR system whose performance is competitive on the standard variety, equitable across dialects, calibrated in its confidences, and reproducible from public artifacts? The answer proposed by the present thesis is that such a combination is possible if heterogeneous teachers are treated as distinct posteriors rather than as competing baselines, if iterative pseudo-labeling is constrained by calibrated confidence, teacher agreement, KL drift, and typological consistency, if dialect, register, and code-switching are unified as latent variables, and if the entire system is anchored in a license-first data substrate.

FINDINGS

Main findings as expected

Pending the completion of the experimental matrix, the main findings anticipated by the present thesis are four. First, the routing of three heterogeneous foundation models outperforms posterior averaging and n-best voting on every evaluation set, with the gain concentrating on segments of intermediate teacher agreement. Second, the typological prior trained on Indonesian, Malay, Cebuano, and Tagalog produces a localized, measurable reduction in WER on low-frequency morphology and rare segmental sequences. Third, the constrained variational EM converges monotonically in held-out loss across iterations, the unconstrained loop demonstrably collapses, and each of the four constraints has a measurable share in the total gain. Fourth, the joint latent inference reduces WER on under-represented dialects and on code-switched speech without degradation on the majority dialect, narrowing the worst-to-best dialect ratio toward the targeted factor of two. The Expected Calibration Error of the calibrated confidence is, throughout, substantially lower than that of the raw confidence, and the calibrator fitted on the supervised set generalizes to the larger, distributionally shifted unlabeled pool.

NOVELTY

Reminder of the novelty

The novelty of the present thesis lies in the unification rather than in any single component taken in isolation. Routing across heterogeneous teachers, typological priors, constrained pseudo-labeling, latent dialect modeling, and post-hoc calibration have each been proposed in earlier literature, often in unrelated contexts. The present work re-reads them as components of a single variational-Bayesian system whose constraints are derived from one another, instantiates that system on a low-resource language for which all five problems are simultaneously load-bearing, and validates the integrated framework through an eight-phase procedure with measurable gates. To that re-reading is added a formal analysis — convergence and non-collapse conditions for the constrained EM — that the empirical literature on iterative pseudo-labeling does not articulate.

LIMITS

Acknowledgment of limits

Five limits condition the interpretation of the contribution. The dialect partition is coarser than the linguistic reality. The calibration set is small in absolute terms. Tier-B annotators see the seed transcription before correcting, introducing an anchoring bias. The constrained EM is iterated under a compute budget rather than to formal convergence. Speech-LLM comparisons may not be available at the date of defense. Each of these limits is reported and, where possible, mitigated by an explicit study.

PERSPECTIVES

Open perspectives

Beyond the present thesis, four perspectives are identified. Cross-lingual transfer — instantiation of the framework on another Austronesian low-resource language to test the generality of the typological prior. On-device deployment — distillation of the integrated system into a sub-100M-parameter student suitable for mobile inference, with continued attention to dialect equity. Speech-LLM integration — the use of a speech-LLM as a downstream rescorer or as an additional teacher in the routing function, conditional on coverage of Malagasy by the LLM's text side. Application studies — deployment trials in education, accessibility, administrative transcription, and journalistic indexing, accompanied by qualitative evaluation. The trajectory beyond the thesis is therefore one of broadening (other languages, other devices) accompanied by deepening (downstream tasks, qualitative evaluation), under a continuous license-first and consent-respecting regime.

CLOSING — The contribution of the present work is offered as a stepping stone: a framework that another doctoral candidate, in another low-resource setting, may pick up, instantiate, and refine. Methodology travels; data does not.

PROVA-MG — Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy.

General conclusion · Doctoral School 3D, University of Toamasina.

Resume & Abstract

French summary and English abstract of the present thesis, each accompanied by five keywords, as required by Doctoral School 3D.

RESUME (FR)

Resume

La presente these aborde le probleme de la reconnaissance automatique de la parole pour le malgache, langue austronesienne classee a faibles ressources, parlee par plus de vingt-cinq millions de locuteurs et caracterisee par au moins dix-huit groupes dialectaux ainsi que par une diglossie marquee avec le francais. Bien que le malgache soit nominalement couvert par les principaux modeles multilingues recents (Whisper, MMS, Wav2Vec2-BERT, XLS-R), les performances en transcription en mode zero-shot restent insuffisantes pour un deploiement, et aucune technique d'adaptation prise isolement ne resout le probleme. La these propose un cadre methodologique unifie, denomme PROVA-MG (Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy), qui aborde la reconnaissance automatique a faibles ressources comme un systeme probabiliste integrant des elements de preuve heterogenes sous calibration explicite et sous contraintes explicites. Cinq composants interconnectes structurent le cadre: la co-inference de trois modeles de fondation traites comme des posteriors distincts; l'integration d'un a priori typologique austronesien dans le decodage; un algorithme EM variationnel contraint pour le pseudo-etiquetage iteratif avec des conditions explicites de non-effondrement; une decomposition a variables latentes du dialecte, du registre et de l'alternance codique; et une tete de calibration post-hoc partagee. Le cadre s'appuie sur un substrat de donnees construit selon une logique licence-first. Une procedure de validation en huit phases avec gates mesurables soutient les pretentions de la these. Les resultats attendus, dont la confirmation est en cours, portent sur la performance globale, l'equite dialectale, la qualite de la calibration et la convergence empirique de la boucle EM contrainte.

Mots cles: reconnaissance automatique de la parole, langues a faibles ressources, malgache, modeles de fondation, EM variationnel contraint.

ABSTRACT (EN)

Abstract

The present thesis addresses the problem of automatic speech recognition for Malagasy, an Austronesian language classified as low-resource, spoken by more than twenty-five million speakers, characterized by at least eighteen dialect groups and by a pronounced diglossia with French. Although Malagasy is nominally covered by the principal recent multilingual models (Whisper, MMS, Wav2Vec2-BERT, XLS-R), zero-shot transcription quality remains below deployment thresholds, and no single adaptation technique resolves the gap. The thesis proposes a unified methodological framework, PROVA-MG (Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy), that approaches low-resource ASR as a probabilistic system aggregating heterogeneous evidence under explicit calibration and explicit constraints. Five interlocking components structure the framework: co-inference of three foundation models treated as distinct posteriors; integration of an Austronesian typological prior into decoding; a constrained variational EM algorithm for iterative pseudo-labeling with explicit non-collapse conditions; a latent-variable decomposition of dialect, register, and code-switching; and a shared post-hoc calibration head. The framework rests on a data substrate constructed under a license-first regime. An eight-phase validation procedure with measurable gates supports the claims of the thesis. The expected results, whose confirmation is in progress, address headline performance, dialect equity, calibration quality, and the empirical convergence of the constrained EM loop.

Keywords: automatic speech recognition, low-resource languages, Malagasy, foundation models, constrained variational EM.

PROVA-MG — Probabilistic Routing Of Variational Alignments for Malagasy.

Annexes

Back matter / Annexes

Eight appendices that document the engineering substrate of the present thesis: local project organization, repository, source code arborescence, launch commands, simulation and production execution, web interface, and execution journal.

ANNEXE A

A. Local project organization in VS Code

The local project organization mirrors the modular structure of the methodology. The Visual Studio Code workspace contains five top-level folders, each corresponding to one segment of the workflow. data/ holds the partitioned manifests for Tier-A, Tier-B, Tier-C, and Tier-D corpora; raw audio is stored on external object storage and referenced by URI from within the manifests. models/ holds the local model registry; foundation checkpoints are referenced as Hugging Face IDs in a JSON index. src/ holds the Python source tree, organized by component (3.1 routing, 3.2 typology, 3.3 EM loop, 3.4 latent inference, 3.5 calibration). experiments/ holds configuration files (YAML) and result manifests (JSONL). docs/ holds the manuscript sources, the model cards, and the datasheets. A .devcontainer/ directory provides a reproducible Docker development image; the IDE attaches to the running container so that the host system is not modified. Linting, type checking, and unit tests run on save through configured tasks.

ANNEXE B

B. Private GitHub repository

The source code, the manifests, the experiment configurations, and the manuscript sources are kept in a private GitHub repository at https://github.com/<org>/prova-mg (URL to be substituted on publication). Access is governed by an explicit collaborator list, recorded in the repository's README. A mirror to an institutional GitLab instance is maintained for continuity. On final defense, a public mirror is created and the artifacts are simultaneously archived on Zenodo with a persistent DOI; the private repository is preserved for change history but is no longer the canonical reference.

ANNEXE D

D. Launch commands

The repository's README.md documents the canonical launch commands for each stage of the workflow. The commands are reproduced below in abbreviated form; the full file in the repository contains environment activation, distributed-launch wrappers, and resume-from-checkpoint flags.

README.md (abbreviated)

# Environment

docker compose up -d devcontainer docker exec -it prova-mg-dev bash

# Stage 1 - initialization

python -m src.common.training --config experiments/configs/initₛup.yaml

# Stage 2 - teacher inference on Tier C python -m src.c31_routing.teachers --teachers all --split tier_c

# Stage 3 - calibration and routing fit

python -m src.c35_calibration.fit_calibrator --config experiments/configs/calib.yaml python -m src.c31_routing.router --config experiments/configs/router.yaml

# Stage 4 - constrained EM loop

python -m src.c33ₑm.run --config experiments/configs/em_full.yaml --iterations 6

# Stage 5 - joint latent inference and final eval python -m src.c34_latent.mean_field --config experiments/configs/latent.yaml

$ python -m src.common.evaluation --splits fleurs_mg cv_mg in_domain

ANNEXE E

E. Execution in simulation mode

For methodological work prior to a full corpus run, a simulation mode is provided. In simulation mode, the unlabeled pool is replaced by a synthetic stream generated from the supervised set by controlled corruption (additive noise, time warping, partial label removal), and the teacher posteriors are emulated by an analytic mixture whose disagreement profile is parameterized. The simulation mode is built on a SimPy-like discrete-event harness and allows the validation of the constrained EM loop independently of compute-heavy teacher inference. A typical simulation log is reproduced below.

simulation.log (excerpt)

[t=0.000] init theta from supervised (N=14 320 segments)

[t=0.001] sim unlabeled stream size=120 000 disagreement_profile=tri-modal

[t=0.014] EM iter 1 E-step: 87.3% segments admitted under C1 C2 C3 C4

[t=0.052] EM iter 1 M-step: held-out WER 31.4 -> 28.9

[t=0.066] EM iter 2 E-step: 88.1% segments admitted

[t=0.108] EM iter 2 M-step: held-out WER 28.9 -> 27.0

[t=0.121] EM iter 3 E-step: 88.6% segments admitted

[t=0.165] EM iter 3 M-step: held-out WER 27.0 -> 26.2

[t=0.166] EM iter 3 KL drift 0.018 < epsilon=0.05 OK

[t=0.220] convergence reached (delta < 0.5 WER)

ANNEXE F

F. Execution in production mode

The production mode runs the same code path on the actual Tier-A through Tier-C corpora and on the registered foundation models. A typical production log records GPU hours, dataset sizes, and per-iteration WER on the held-out development set. Logs are stored under experiments/results/<run_id>/ and indexed by Weights & Biases.

ANNEXE G

G. Web interface

A small web interface, served from a FastAPI back-end and a Svelte front-end, exposes the final model for interactive testing. The interface accepts a recorded or uploaded audio segment, displays the top-1 transcript together with the calibrated confidence and the per-teacher transcripts, shows the inferred dialect and register, and highlights segments tagged as code-switched. A screenshot, reproduced in the printed thesis, displays the layout: a recording widget at the top, the consensus transcription in the centre with confidence-coloured highlighting, the three teacher transcripts side by side below, and a metadata bar at the bottom reporting dialect, register, code-switching density, and a link to the segment-level posterior visualization. The interface is intended primarily for qualitative diagnostic rather than for production deployment.

ANNEXE H

H. Execution journal

A daily execution journal is kept throughout the doctoral period as a tab-separated text file under version control. Each entry records the date, the active stage of the workflow, the run identifiers launched, the experiment configurations modified, the issues encountered, and the resolution. APPENDIX — WORKING MATERIAL

Appendix A — Plain-Algebra Primer to the PROVA-MG Formulas

PROVA-MG / A guided climb from basic algebra

Understanding PROVA-MG, one symbol at a time

If you can read “x + 2 = 5, so x = 3”, you already know enough to start. This page adds exactly one new idea at a time until the final, novel formula at the bottom is something you can read out loud and actually mean.

HOW TO READ THIS PAGE

Every formula in the thesis is built from a handful of small ideas stacked on top of each other. We introduce those ideas in order. Nothing below assumes more than school algebra; every new piece of notation gets defined the moment it appears.

Each step has four parts: the new idea in words, the symbol written in real mathematical notation, a worked micro-example with actual numbers, and a plain-English reading so you never decode a formula alone. A running “what we can read so far” bar tracks your progress.

THE DESTINATION — The goal of the whole project: teach a computer to turn Malagasy speech into written text, even though almost no labelled Malagasy audio exists. The final formula is the rule the system follows so it can teach itself from unlabelled audio without fooling itself.

STEP 0

A letter is just a box that holds a value

In algebra, x is a placeholder for something we don’t know yet. That is the only trick, and it never goes away — it only gets dressed up. In this project the placeholders hold richer things than plain numbers:

SymbolWhat is in the box
xthe audio — the sound recording (a chunk of speech)
ythe text — the transcription of what was said
dthe dialect (Merina, Betsimisaraka, Sakalava, …)
rthe register (read aloud, broadcast, conversation, ceremony)
cthe code-switching tag (Malagasy, French, or mixed)
θ(“theta”) all the knobs of the model — the numbers learning will adjust

Whenever you see one of these letters, say its plain name in your head: x → “the audio”, y → “the text”. Greek letters are not special — they are just letters used so we don’t run out: θ (theta), α (alpha), β (beta), τ (tau), ε (epsilon), η (eta), λ (lambda), φ (phi), μ (mu) all appear below, and each is introduced where it is first used.

So far we can read: x, y, d, r, c, θ — six labelled boxes.

STEP 1

A function is a machine: put something in, get something out

You already met functions as f(x) — “f of x” — a machine that takes x and returns a value. Read the parentheses as “applied to”. Everything later of the form g(stuff) means exactly this: a machine applied to whatever sits in the parentheses.

f(x) = 2x + 1

WORKED EXAMPLE — Put in x = 3: f(3) = 2· 3 + 1 = 7. Put in x = 10: f(10) = 21. A function is a promise: the same input always gives the same output.

A function can take several inputs at once, separated by commas: g(a, b) is “g applied to a and b together.” Later we will see conf_(cal)(y, x), which is simply a machine fed two boxes — a text and an audio — returning one number.

So far we can read: boxes, and f(·) = a machine applied to whatever sits in the parentheses.

STEP 2

Probability: a number between 0 and 1 for “how likely”

We write p(·) for “the probability of”. It is just a function whose output is always in the range [0, 1]: 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, 0.5 means coin-flip.

0 ≤ p(y) ≤ 1 where p(y) means “how likely is the text y?”

Two short extensions you must recognise, both ordinary algebra:

  • Joint — p(x, y): “how likely is it that this audio and this text happen together?” The comma means “and”.
  • Conditional — p(y | x): “given that we already have the audio x, how likely is the text y?” The bar | means “given” / “assuming we already know”.

These are tied together by one rule you may remember — the definition of conditional probability:

p(y | x) = (p(x, y))/(p(x))

WORKED EXAMPLE — Of all recordings, suppose 2% are a particular sentence and a clear recording: p(x,y) = 0.02. Suppose 10% of recordings are that clear: p(x) = 0.10. Then given a clear recording, the chance it is that sentence is p(y| x) = 0.02 / 0.10 = 0.20, i.e. 20%.

READ IT OUT LOUD — p(y | x) = “the chance the text is y, given the recording x.” This single object — chance of the text given the sound — is what every ASR system is ultimately trying to compute.

So far we can read: p(y) a chance, p(x,y) chance of both, p(y| x) chance of y given x.

STEP 3

Multiplying chances = a chain of “and”s — the generative model

When several things all have to happen, you multiply their chances. Two coins both landing heads: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. More precisely, a joint probability can always be unrolled into a chain of conditionals (the “chain rule”):

p(a, b) = p(a) p(b | a)

The thesis imagines how a recording is “born”, one factor at a time, and multiplies them. This is the first real formula from the paper — the generative model:

p(x, y, d, r, c) = p(d) p(r) p(c | r, d) p(y | d, r, c) p(x | y, d, r)

READING IT LEFT TO RIGHT (COMMA = “AND”, BAR = “GIVEN”) — “The chance of this whole situation = pick a dialect p(d) × pick a register p(r) × decide the language mix given dialect & register p(c| r,d) × produce the text given all that p(y| d,r,c) × finally produce the sound given the text, dialect and register p(x| y,d,r).”

The shape of this product encodes real modelling choices: dialect d and register r are written as independent factors p(d) p(r) because a Merina speaker can be recorded either reading aloud or chatting; but the language mix c is conditioned on both, p(c | r, d), because code-switching is socially structured.

Plain comparison: it is like subtitling that simultaneously guesses what was said, in which accent, in which setting (radio? chat?), and whether the sentence mixes French and Malagasy. Each guess feeds the next, and we multiply how likely each guess is.

So far we can read: a product of chances describing how audio+text is generated. One full paper formula down.

STEP 4

Logarithms: turn hard multiplication into easy addition

Multiplying many tiny probabilities gives absurdly small numbers that computers round to zero. The fix is the logarithm, written log . Its one magic property is all you need:

log (A × B) = log A + log B and log A/B = log A - log B

WORKED EXAMPLE — Three probabilities 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125. In logs (base 10): log 0.5 ≈ -0.30, so the sum is -0.30 - 0.30 - 0.30 = -0.90, and indeed log 0.125 ≈ -0.90. A messy product became a clean sum.

WHY WE BOTHER — “log of a product = sum of the logs.” So every multiplication from Step 3 becomes a tidy addition. That is the only reason log appears everywhere below — it is a convenience, not a new concept.

One side note: probabilities are below 1, so their logs are negative. “Bigger” (closer to 0) still means “more likely”. Don’t let the minus signs scare you: -0.9 is more likely than -5.0.

So far we can read: log turns × into +, so “most likely” becomes “biggest sum”.

STEP 5

Decoding: add up the evidence and keep the best text

Now combine Steps 2–4. To transcribe, the system scores each candidate text by adding three kinds of log-evidence. This is the project’s decoding rule:

log P(y | x) ∝ log P_(acoustic)(x | y) + α log P_(LM-MG)(y) + β log P_(typ)(y)

PiecePlain meaning
log P_(acoustic)(x | y)“does the sound match this text?”
log P_(LM-MG)(y)“is this good Malagasy on its own?”
log P_(typ)(y)“does it fit the cousin languages (Indonesian, Malay, Tagalog…)?”
α, βplain dials (just numbers ≥ 0) setting how much to trust the last two clues
∝“proportional to” — equal up to a constant we don’t care about when ranking

WORKED EXAMPLE — Two candidate texts y₁, y₂. Say the sound favours y₁ (-2.0 vs -2.3), but y₂ is far better Malagasy (αlog P_(LM): -0.2 vs -1.5). With α = 1, β = 0: score(y₁) = -3.5, score(y₂) = -2.5. So y₂ wins — the language clue overruled a slightly better sound match.

IN WORDS — “A text’s score = how well it matches the sound + (a little) how Malagasy it sounds + (a little) how Austronesian its shape is.” The α and β dials balance the three voices. Comparison: learning Italian faster by leaning on Spanish and Portuguese.

So far we can read: a weighted sum of log-evidence that ranks candidate transcriptions.

STEP 6

argmax and argmin: “which choice wins?”

Two pieces of notation that look intimidating but mean something everyday.

  • argmax — “the input that makes this biggest.” Not the biggest value, but which choice produces it. (“Who scored the most points?” → the person, not the score.)
  • argmin — the same, but the input that makes it smallest.

ŷ = argmax_y [ score(y) ]

WORKED EXAMPLE — If score(y₁) = -3.5, score(y₂) = -2.5, score(y₃) = -4.1, then max of the scores is -2.5, but argmax is y₂ — the text, not the number. The little y under the operator says “we are choosing among the y’s.” The hat in ̂y means “our chosen estimate”.

IN WORDS — “Out of all possible texts y, hand me the one with the highest score.” That is decoding: argmax over the rule from Step 5.

So far we can read: argmax = the choice that wins; argmin = the choice that loses-least.

STEP 7

Sums and the average machine E (expected value)

First, the summation sign ∑ is just “add these up.” ∑ᵢ aᵢ = a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + … Nothing more.

The symbol E (a fancy E) means average — the typical outcome if you weight every possibility by how likely it is. In plain algebra it is exactly a weighted sum of value × chance:

E_q[ s(y) ] = ∑_y q(y) s(y)

WORKED EXAMPLE — A die pays s = 1 on a six and s = 0 otherwise, with fair odds q = 1/6 each face. Then E_q[s] = 1/6· 1 + 5/6· 0 = 1/6 ≈ 0.17 — the long-run average payout.

IN WORDS — “If you tried this many times following the odds q, what would you get on average?” The little q under E just says which set of odds to average with.

So far we can read: ∑ = add up; E_q[·] = the average of something under the odds q.

STEP 8

KL: a number for “how different are two opinions?”

Often we have two sets of odds — the model’s guess q and some target p — and want to know how far apart they are. The KL divergence KL(q ‖ p) is that gap as a single number. It is built from the pieces you already have (a sum, a log, an average):

KL( q ‖ p ) = ∑_y q(y) log (q(y))/(p(y)) = E_q[ log (q(y))/(p(y)) ] ≥ 0

The key facts: it is never negative, and it equals exactly 0 only when q and p are identical. Bigger means more disagreement. (The double bar ‖ is just punctuation separating the two distributions.)

WORKED EXAMPLE — If q = p everywhere, each term is q(y)log 1 = 0, so KL = 0 — no disagreement. The more q puts weight where p does not, the larger the positive total grows.

IN WORDS — “How surprised would you be if you trusted q but reality followed p?” You don’t need to memorise the formula — only that it is a distance between two probability opinions, never negative, zero when they match.

So far we can read: KL(q ‖ p) = how far guess q is from target p (0 = perfect match).

STEP 9A

A safety net under the goal: the ELBO

We would love to maximise log p(x, y) directly — “make the data the model actually saw as likely as possible.” But the hidden variables d, r, c make that sum impossible to compute exactly. The standard trick is to maximise a guaranteed lower floor beneath it instead, called the evidence lower bound (ELBO):

log p(x, y) ≥ L_(ELBO)(θ, φ) = E_q[ log p_θ(x, y, d, r, c) ] [fit the data well] - KL( q_φ ‖ p ) [stay honest]

≥“is at least” — the ELBO sits below the thing we want, so pushing it up drags the real goal up too
θthe knobs of the generative model (Step 3)
φ(“phi”) the knobs of the guesser q — the network that proposes the hidden answers

IN WORDS — “Raise a floor you can compute, made of two pieces: a reward for fitting the data (first term) minus a penalty for the guesser drifting away from what’s plausible (the KL term). Push the floor up and the true goal rises with it.”

So far we can read: the ELBO = (fit the data) − (KL honesty penalty), a floor we maximise instead of the impossible exact goal.

STEP 9B

EM: guess the hidden parts, then improve — repeat

Here is the engine that climbs that floor. We have audio but, for most of it, no human transcription — and we never directly see the dialect, register or language-mix. Those are hidden. The EM algorithm handles “learn from data with missing pieces” by alternating two moves until things settle:

  • E-step (Estimate): with the current knobs θ, guess the hidden pieces. Using Step 8’s tool: pick the guess-odds q that are closest (smallest KL) to what the model currently believes about x.
  • M-step (Maximise): treat those guesses as if they were true labels, and adjust the knobs θ to fit them as well as possible (argmax of the average log-likelihood from Step 7).

E-step: q^* = argmin_q KL( q ‖ p_θ( · | x) ) M-step: θ ← argmax_θ E_(q^*)[ log p_θ(x, y, d, r, c) ]

q^*the best current guess of the hidden pieces (the star ^* = “the winning one”)
p_θ(· | x)what the model, with knobs θ, currently believes about the hidden pieces given x
←“becomes” — replace the old knobs with this new value

IN WORDS — E-step: “with today’s knobs, make the best guess of the missing answers.” M-step: “turn the knobs so those guesses become as likely as possible.” Loop. Comparison: a student grading their own homework to improve — each round a little better. Every loop is guaranteed not to lower the ELBO of Step 9a.

So far we can read the whole EM loop: guess hidden answers (E), then retune knobs θ to fit them (M), repeat.

STEP 10

The danger that makes this hard: self-delusion

A student who grades their own homework can drift into confidently marking wrong answers right, then studying from them — getting surer and worse at the same time. In machine learning this is called collapse, and it is exactly what kills naive self-training: the model’s confidence inflates while its accuracy degrades. The novel contribution of PROVA-MG is to bolt four guard-rails onto the E-step so the loop cannot fool itself.

THE WHOLE IDEA IN ONE LINE — Keep EM’s self-teaching power, but only let it learn from guesses that are (C1) honestly confident, (C2) not a wild swing from last round, (C3) backed by other models, and (C4) shaped like a real Austronesian word.

STEP 11

The four guard-rails, each a small inequality

Each guard-rail is just an algebra inequality (≥ “at least”, ≤ “no more than”). Together they define a set of allowed guesses, written C. Read each one slowly — you already know every symbol.

• C1 — honest confidence. Keep a transcript only if its calibrated confidence clears a threshold τ (“tau”, a chosen number like 0.8).

supp(q^*) ⊂ { y : conf_(cal)(y, x) ≥ τ }

supp(q^*)the “support” — the texts our guess actually puts any weight on
⊂“is contained within”
{ y : … }“the set of all y such that …”
conf_(cal)confidence that has been reality-checked (calibrated), not raw bravado

IN WORDS — “Every text we keep must have calibrated confidence at least τ.” We ignore the student who says “99% sure” but is wrong half the time.

• C2 — no whiplash. From one round n to the next n+1, the guesses may only drift a little — the average KL gap (Step 8) stays under a small ε (“epsilon”, a tiny number).

Eₓ[ KL( q^((n+1))( · | x) ‖ q^((n))( · | x) ) ] ≤ ε

IN WORDS — “On average across all audio x, this round’s opinion must stay close to last round’s.” A doctor revises a diagnosis gradually, not overnight. The superscripts ^((n)) and ^((n+1)) just label “this round” and “next round.”

• C3 — second opinions. The kept answer must also appear in the short-lists (“n-best”) of the independent teacher models — Whisper (W), MMS (M), Wav2Vec2-BERT (B).

supp(q^*) ∩ ( n-best_W ∪ n-best_M ∪ n-best_B ) ≠ ∅

∩“overlap with” (intersection)
∪“pooled together” (union)
≠ ∅“is not empty” — i.e. there is overlap

IN WORDS — “Our chosen text must show up on at least one independent expert’s short-list.” Keep only what other models also propose — they have different blind spots, so agreement is informative.

• C4 — it must look like a real word. On average, the typological score (“does this fit Austronesian sound-patterns?”) must stay above a floor -η (“eta”).

E_(q^*)[ log P_(typ)(y) ] ≥ -η

IN WORDS — “The kept transcripts must, on average, be phonetically plausible for the language family.” A French speaker feels “travu” could be French while “tlbvk” could not — even never having seen either. We throw out the “tlbvk” cases. (Not about whether a word exists elsewhere — Malagasy has plenty of its own words — but whether its shape is possible.)

Bundle all four into one name: C = { q : q satisfies C1 and C2 and C3 and C4 } — “the set of guesses that pass every guard-rail.”

So far we can read: four plain inequalities C1–C4, and the allowed-guess set C = all four at once.

STEP 12 — THE SUMMIT

The final, novel formula — read it like a sentence

Everything you have learned now snaps together. Take the EM loop from Step 9b, and in the E-step add three little symbols under the argmin: q ∈ C — “choose only among guesses that obey the four guard-rails.” That single restriction is the contribution.

E-step: q^* = argmin_(q ∈ C) KL( q ‖ p_θ( · | x) ) [4pt] M-step: θ ← argmax_θ E_(q^*)[ log p_θ(x, y, d, r, c) ] + λ R(θ)

NOW READ THE WHOLE THING IN PLAIN ENGLISH — E-step: “Among only the guesses that are honestly confident, not a wild swing, backed by other models, and shaped like a real word (q ∈ C), pick the one (argmin) closest (smallest KL) to what the model currently believes about the audio.”

M-step: “Then turn the model’s knobs θ (argmax) so those trusted guesses become as likely (highest average log-chance) as possible — plus a tidiness term λ R(θ) that stops the knobs from going to extremes.”

Then loop. Because of q ∈ C, every round can only learn from trustworthy guesses, so it gets better without the self-delusion of Step 10.

Last new symbolsPlain meaning
q ∈ Cthe novel part: “q must be inside the allowed-guess set C” — obey all four guard-rails
λ R(θ)a gentle “don’t overdo it” penalty: R scores how extreme the knobs are, λ (lambda) sets how strict that penalty is

WHAT MAKES IT NOVEL — Plain EM has been known for decades. The contribution is the two characters ∈ C: forcing the self-teaching loop to draw only from guesses that pass four independent sanity checks — calibrated confidence (C1), bounded drift (C2), cross-model agreement (C3), and typological plausibility (C4). That turns a loop that usually collapses into one that is provably stable for low-resource Malagasy.

You can now read the final formula end to end:
boxes (x,y,d,r,c,θ) → functions f(·) → chances p(·) → products of chances → log turns × into + → weighted-sum decoding → argmax/argmin pick the winner → ∑ and E average → KL measures disagreement → ELBO floor → EM guesses-then-improves → four guard-rails C → constrained variational EM.

BONUS — WHERE THE CALIBRATED CONFIDENCE COMES FROM

One more formula you can now read: calibration

Guard-rail C1 relied on a calibrated confidence. Where does that honesty come from? A small extra model g_φ is trained so its reported confidence matches the real hit-rate. Its training objective is, once more, only pieces you know — a sum of logs plus a tidiness penalty:

L_(cal)(φ) = -∑_((x,y) ∈ Dₛᵤₚ) log g_φ( features(x), 1[ ŷ(x) = y ] ) + μ ‖ g_φ ‖²

Dₛᵤₚthe small supervised set where we do have correct transcripts to check against
1[ ̂y(x) = y]an “indicator”: 1 if the guess was right, 0 if wrong
μ ‖ g_φ ‖²(“mu”) the same kind of tidiness penalty as λ R(θ), keeping the calibrator smooth

IN WORDS — “Tune the confidence-model φ so that, on the cases where we know the answer, its stated confidence lines up with how often it’s actually right — and keep it simple.” This is what makes C1’s threshold τ meaningful.

ONE-LINE SUMMARY

Three teacher models + cousin-language hints + honest confidence, combined by an EM loop that may only learn from guesses passing four guard-rails C — which is what makes its self-training provably non-collapsing.

WHERE TO GO NEXT — Ready for the full treatment? See Chapter III — The PROVA-MG Methodology for the complete derivation, complexity analysis and pseudocode, or the essential FR summary for the same ideas in French.

Appendix B — Nouvelle méthodologie (résumé en français)

PROVA-MG / L’essentiel · FR

La nouvelle méthodologie , en bref

L’idée centrale et les mathématiques strictement nécessaires.

L’IDÉE

On combine trois modèles ASR existants (Whisper, MMS, Wav2Vec2-BERT), une connaissance des langues cousines du malgache, et une mesure honnête de la confiance, sous quatre garde-fous qui empêchent le système de s’auto-persuader d’erreurs.

Comparaison : comme un jury de trois médecins qui ne valident un diagnostic que si (a) ils sont sûrs d’eux pour de bonnes raisons, (b) ils ne changent pas d’avis du jour au lendemain, (c) au moins deux sont d’accord, et (d) le diagnostic est plausible médicalement.

LE MODÈLE

Le signal x et la transcription y sont engendrés avec trois variables cachées : dialecte d, registre r, code-switching c.

p(x, y, d, r, c) = p(d) p(r) p(c | r, d) p(y | d, r, c) p(x | y, d, r)

Comparaison : comme un sous-titrage qui devine en même temps ce qui est dit, dans quel accent, dans quel contexte (radio ? conversation ?), et si la phrase mélange français et malgache.

L’APPRENTISSAGE

On alterne deux étapes (algorithme EM). L’étape E estime les variables cachées sous contraintes ; l’étape M ajuste les paramètres.

E-step : q^* = argmin_(q ∈ C) KL( q ‖ p_θ( · | x) ) M-step : θ ← argmax_θ E_(q^*)[ log p_θ(x, y, d, r, c) ]

Comparaison : comme un élève qui corrige ses devoirs lui-même pour progresser — mais soumis à des règles qui l’empêchent d’inventer ses propres réponses.

LES QUATRE GARDE-FOUS (LE CŒUR DE LA CONTRIBUTION)

Sans contraintes, l’auto-entraînement s’effondre : le modèle devient de plus en plus sûr de plus en plus de mauvaises réponses. Chaque règle ferme une porte de sortie.

• C1 — seuil de confiance calibrée. N’accepter que les transcriptions dont la confiance est réellement justifiée. Comparaison : on ignore un élève qui dit « je suis sûr à 99 % » mais qui se trompe une fois sur deux.

supp(q^*) ⊂ { y : conf_(cal)(y, x) ≥ τ }

• C2 — vitesse limitée. D’une itération à la suivante, le modèle ne peut pas changer radicalement d’avis. Comparaison : un médecin révise un diagnostic graduellement, pas brutalement.

Eₓ[ KL( q^((n+1)) ‖ q^((n)) ) ] ≤ ε

• C3 — accord des enseignants. La réponse retenue doit apparaître dans la liste de plusieurs des trois modèles enseignants. Comparaison : on ne retient que ce sur quoi au moins deux experts indépendants tombent d’accord.

supp(q^*) ∩ ( n-best_W ∪ n-best_M ∪ n-best_B ) ≠ ∅

• C4 — plausibilité linguistique. Les transcriptions dont la forme (enchaînements de sons, schémas d’affixes) ne ressemble à aucune langue austronésienne sont rejetées. Il ne s’agit pas de vérifier qu’un mot existe ailleurs — le malgache a quantité de mots qui lui sont propres — mais qu’il aurait pu exister vu la structure de la famille. Comparaison : un francophone sent que « travu » pourrait être un mot français alors que « tlbvk » ne le pourrait pas — même sans l’avoir jamais vu. On écarte les transcriptions de type « tlbvk ».

E_(q^*)[ log P_(typ)(y) ] ≥ -η

DÉCODAGE AVEC A PRIORI TYPOLOGIQUE

On utilise les langues cousines du malgache (indonésien, malais, cebuano, tagalog) pour combler le manque de données :

log P(y | x) ∝ log P_(acoustique)(x | y) + α log P_(LM-MG)(y) + β log P_(typ)(y)

Comparaison : apprendre l’italien plus vite en s’aidant de l’espagnol et du portugais.

EN UNE LIGNE — Trois enseignants + a priori cousins + confiance calibrée, combinés par un EM variationnel sous quatre contraintes qui rendent la boucle d’auto-entraînement prouvablement non-dérivante.
